title: Vertical $β$-Ga$_2$O$_3$ Schottky Diodes with Deep-Etch Field Termination using Plasma-free Ga-assisted Etching
summary: A deep-etch field termination strategy using a Ga-assisted plasma-free etching technique in a low-pressure chemical vapor deposition (LPCVD) system is demonstrated for $β$-Ga$_2$O$_3$ Schottky barrier diodes (SBDs). The thermally activated etching method provides a plasma-free approach for forming deep mesa terminations while maintaining excellent device integrity. The fabricated diodes exhibit excellent forward conduction characteristics with a turn-on voltage of 1.14~V, a Schottky barrier height (SBH) of 1.15~eV, an ideality factor of 1.20, and a specific on-resistance of 3.72~m$Ω\cdot$cm$^2$, all closely matching those of the unetched planar devices. Capacitance-voltage analysis further confirms a uniform carrier concentration of $2\times10^{16}$~cm$^{-3}$ and an SBH of 1.23~eV, indicating stable electrical characteristics after deep mesa formation. Temperature-dependent electrical measurements from 25 to 250$^\circ$C demonstrate stable thermionic-emission transport behavior, with a gradual increase in on-resistance at elevated temperatures due to phonon-limited carrier mobility. Over this temperature range, the SBH decreases from 1.16 to 1.12~eV, while the ideality factor increases from 1.21 to 1.33. The leakage current remains low throughout the entire temperature range, and the rectification ratio remains above $10^{5}$ even at 250$^\circ$C. Under reverse bias, the diodes exhibit an increase in breakdown voltage from 287V to 500V, confirming the effectiveness of geometric electric-field redistribution achieved by the deep-etched mesa structure. Silvaco TCAD simulations corroborate these experimental observations by showing significant suppression of electric-field crowding near the anode edge. These results establish Ga-assisted plasma-free etching as a reliable, damage-free field termination technique for high-performance $β$-Ga$_2$O$_3$ power devices.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates a Ga-assisted plasma-free deep-etch field termination technique for β-Ga₂O₃ Schottky barrier diodes, achieving excellent electrical performance (low on-resistance, high rectification ratio >10⁵ at 250°C, and improved breakdown voltage from 287V to 500V) with TCAD validation, establishing a damage-free method for high-power Ga₂O₃ devices.
AI.motivation: To develop a plasma-free, damage-free deep mesa etching technique for β-Ga₂O₃ SBDs that effectively terminates electric fields and enhances breakdown voltage while preserving device integrity, overcoming the limitations of conventional plasma-based etching methods.
AI.method: Ga-assisted plasma-free etching in an LPCVD system was used to form deep mesa terminations. Electrical characterization (I-V, C-V, temperature-dependent measurements from 25–250°C) and Silvaco TCAD simulations were performed to evaluate device performance and electric field redistribution.
AI.result: Diodes showed a turn-on voltage of 1.14V, SBH of 1.15–1.23 eV, ideality factor of 1.20, specific on-resistance of 3.72 mΩ·cm², breakdown voltage increased from 287V to 500V, rectification ratio >10⁵ at 250°C, and stable thermionic-emission transport with minimal leakage.
AI.conclusion: Ga-assisted plasma-free etching is a reliable, damage-free field termination technique that significantly enhances breakdown voltage while maintaining excellent forward characteristics, suitable for high-performance β-Ga₂O₃ power devices.

title: Limitations of Classical Force Fields for Metal Coordination Modes in Proteins: A Multilevel Study of Ca$^{2+}$ in Integrin $α_Vβ_3$
summary: Standard biomolecular force fields often present limitations in modeling metal coordination modes. Here, we combined classical and QM/MM molecular dynamics simulations to investigate the Ca$^{2+}$ mediated binding of cRGD to integrin $α_Vβ_3$. The results demonstrate the inherent limitations of fixed-point-charge force fields in reproducing asymmetric binding modes and highlight the value of QM-based multilevel approaches to assess the correctness and accuracy of FF models and capture metal coordination modes in complex biomolecular systems.

AI.tldr: This study uses classical and QM/MM MD simulations to investigate Ca²⁺-mediated cRGD binding to integrin αVβ3, revealing limitations of fixed-point-charge force fields in reproducing asymmetric metal coordination and demonstrating the value of QM-based multilevel approaches for accurate modeling.
AI.motivation: Standard biomolecular force fields have inherent limitations in modeling metal coordination modes, motivating the need to assess their accuracy and develop improved approaches for such complex biomolecular systems.
AI.method: Combined classical molecular dynamics (MD) and QM/MM (quantum mechanics/molecular mechanics) molecular dynamics simulations.
AI.result: Fixed-point-charge force fields exhibit inherent limitations in reproducing asymmetric binding modes of Ca²⁺-mediated cRGD-integrin interactions.
AI.conclusion: QM-based multilevel approaches are valuable for assessing the correctness and accuracy of force field models and for capturing metal coordination modes in complex biomolecular systems.

title: Sub-Terahertz Channel Performance under Snowfall
comment: Submitted to IEEE Transactions on Terahertz Science and Technology
summary: The terahertz (THz) band promises terabit-per-second links but is highly sensitive to snowfall. Natural snowflakes are non-spherical. Yet existing THz studies treat them as spheres under Mie theory, and no ITU-R model covers THz snow attenuation. This work combines line-of-sight measurements at 120, 140, and 160 GHz with physics-based scattering modeling. The measured loss is compared against the ITU-R P.1817-1 optical model, Mie models, and a discrete dipole approximation (DDA) for randomly oriented hexagonal-plate ice crystals, each with the Scott and Gunn-Marshall size distributions. Over the measured band, ITU-R P.1817-1 overestimates and the Mie models underestimate the loss. The shape-aware DDA-Scott model agrees best, with the lowest RMSE at every frequency. From DDA-Scott, we derive a compact modified ITU-R expression in carrier frequency and liquid-water-equivalent (LWE) rate. It reproduces the reference to within 2.5 dB/km over 100-500 GHz and 0-3 mm/h. A Rician K-factor analysis shows the channel stays LoS-dominated, so snowfall degrades the link mainly through attenuation, not multipath fading. A QPSK/16-QAM link-budget analysis then quantifies the cost of the spherical assumption. Mie-based margins overestimate the tolerable snowfall rate by 3.4 across 120-160 GHz, rising toward 5.8 in the upper transparency windows by model extrapolation. The model is further mapped into snow-limited range and adaptive-modulation switching boundaries. These results support future ITU-R recommendations for THz channels under snowfall.

AI.tldr: The paper challenges the widespread spherical-snowflake assumption in THz channel modeling by showing, through measurements at 120-160 GHz and shape-aware DDA modeling, that hexagonal-plate ice crystals with the Scott size distribution best capture snow attenuation, while the existing ITU-R optical model overestimates and Mie models underestimate loss; the authors derive a compact modified ITU-R expression that is accurate over 100-500 GHz/0-3 mm/h, and quantify that spherical assumptions overestimate tolerable snowfall rates by a factor of 3.4-5.8.
AI.motivation: The THz band is highly sensitive to snowfall for future terabit-per-second links, but natural snowflakes are non-spherical and no existing ITU-R model covers THz snow attenuation; previous studies incorrectly treat snowflakes as spheres under Mie theory.
AI.method: Line-of-sight measurements at 120, 140, and 160 GHz combined with physics-based scattering modeling using DDA for randomly oriented hexagonal-plate ice crystals, compared against ITU-R P.1817-1, Mie models, and two size distributions (Scott and Gunn-Marshall).
AI.result: ITU-R P.1817-1 overestimates and Mie models underestimate loss; DDA-Scott achieves lowest RMSE across all frequencies; spherical assumptions overestimate tolerable snowfall rate by factors of 3.4-5.8; channel remains LoS-dominated with snowfall degrading mainly through attenuation rather than multipath fading.
AI.conclusion: A compact modified ITU-R expression derived from DDA-Scott reproduces reference loss to within 2.5 dB/km over 100-500 GHz/0-3 mm/h, supporting future ITU-R recommendations for THz channels under snowfall with snow-limited range and adaptive-modulation switching boundaries.

title: Geometric Algebra Meets Cartesian Tensors: Higher-Order Equivariance for Interatomic Potentials
summary: $\mathrm{Cl}(3,0)$ interatomic potentials, despite their algebraic elegance, predict force magnitudes accurately but force directions poorly. Across ten rMD17 molecules, every $L \leq 1$ baseline in our twelve-model study attains aggregate force-cosine similarity below $0.25$. The cause is structural. The geometric product of two vectors in $\mathbb{R}^3$ realises only the $L=0$ and $L=1$ components of its irreducible representation content, leaving the symmetric-traceless rank-2 component absent from the per-edge bilinear that drives each message-passing layer. We address this with CliffordSTF, which couples the Clifford multivector to closed-form symmetric-traceless tensor tracks at ranks two and three through bilinear cross-track contractions, using a single learned bilinear and no Clebsch--Gordan tables, Wigner-$D$ matrices, or e3nn calls. On rMD17, CliffordSTF raises aggregate force-cosine similarity from $0.055$ (base Clifford) to $0.551$, an order-of-magnitude relative directional gain, alongside improved magnitude accuracy (force MAE $15.8\%$ lower; energy MAE $10.9\%$ lower). It outperforms all CG-free or body-ordered baselines in our study (all $\leq 0.17$). On catalysis benchmarks, CliffordSTF achieves the best out-of-distribution S2EF energy MAE on OC22 in our experiments, and the best in-distribution energy MAE among $L \geq 2$ methods on OC22 IS2RE. An eleven-variant ablation shows the two tracks are complementary: neither alone matches the combined model.

AI.tldr: CliffordSTF enhances Clifford interatomic potentials by adding symmetric-traceless tensor tracks (ranks 2 and 3), dramatically improving force direction accuracy (cosine similarity from 0.055 to 0.551) and reducing force/energy errors, outperforming CG-free baselines on rMD17 and achieving state-of-the-art on OC22 catalysis benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Standard Cl(3,0) interatomic potentials predict force magnitudes accurately but force directions poorly (cosine similarity < 0.25) because the geometric product of two vectors realizes only L=0 and L=1 irreducible representations, missing the symmetric-traceless rank-2 component necessary for accurate directional force predictions.
AI.method: CliffordSTF couples the Clifford multivector to closed-form symmetric-traceless tensor tracks at ranks two and three via bilinear cross-track contractions, using a single learned bilinear without Clebsch-Gordan tables, Wigner-D matrices, or e3nn.
AI.result: On rMD17: force-cosine similarity improves from 0.055 to 0.551 (10x relative gain); force MAE 15.8% lower; energy MAE 10.9% lower. Outperforms all CG-free/body-ordered baselines (≤0.17). On OC22: best out-of-distribution S2EF energy MAE and best in-distribution IS2RE energy MAE among L≥2 methods.
AI.conclusion: The two complementary tensor tracks are necessary—neither alone matches the combined model—and CliffordSTF provides an efficient, CG-free solution to the structural directional limitations of Clifford interatomic potentials.

title: Design and Realization of Broadband Magnonic Spectrometers With Local Electrical Outputs
summary: Microscopic radio-frequency (RF) devices based on propagating spin waves (SWs) are promising for compact, energy-efficient RF signal processing, but their implementation is impeded by fabrication complexity and the lack of efficient electrical readout. In this work, we demonstrate a SW-based Rowland circle spectrometer with electrical input and local electrical output transducers. The device is realized using a scalable fabrication process based on sputter deposition and wet-chemical etching of Yttrium-Iron-Garnet (YIG), forming concave grating structures with micrometer-scale features. The device functionality is confirmed by combined electrical and magneto-optical measurements, which show that the deflection of SW wavefronts at different input frequencies closely follows the analytically predicted behavior. The linear excitation of SWs via two input tones further confirms the spectrometer operation for simultaneously propagating waves. Beyond the single-device demonstration, we propose a concept for scalable architectures comprising multiple Rowland circles with tunable operating points. When combined with broadband parallel electrical readout, this approach enables control over bandwidth and spectral resolution, which are relevant to spectral occupancy detection in wireless communication systems.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates a spin-wave-based Rowland circle spectrometer fabricated using scalable sputter deposition and wet-chemical etching of YIG, featuring electrical input/output transducers. It confirms device operation via electrical and magneto-optical measurements, and proposes scalable multi-circle architectures for tunable spectral analysis in wireless communications.
AI.motivation: Microscopic RF devices based on propagating spin waves are promising for compact, energy-efficient signal processing, but their implementation is hindered by fabrication complexity and lack of efficient electrical readout.
AI.method: The device is realized via scalable fabrication (sputter deposition + wet-chemical etching of YIG) forming concave grating structures. Combined electrical and magneto-optical measurements validate functionality. A scalable architecture with multiple Rowland circles and parallel electrical readout is proposed.
AI.result: SW wavefront deflection at different input frequencies matches analytical predictions. Linear two-tone excitation confirms simultaneous spectrometer operation. The proposed multi-circle architecture enables control over bandwidth and spectral resolution.
AI.conclusion: This work overcomes key fabrication and readout challenges for SW-based RF spectrometers, and the scalable architecture offers a path toward practical spectral occupancy detection in wireless communication systems.

title: Thermal Fundamental Gap Predictions in DFT via Optimally Tuned Hybrids
summary: Predicting electronic fundamental gaps at finite temperature has remained conceptually and practically challenging. We address this in three connected steps. First, we extend generalized Kohn--Sham hybrid density functional theory to thermal ensembles, deriving a Mermin generalized Kohn--Sham framework from a thermal one-particle auxiliary system and an exact density-functional remainder. Second, via an extension of Janak's theorem that holds rigorously in this framework, we recast Hirata's thermal-quasiparticle picture as a thermal orbital gap estimator and derive a closed low-temperature form, the error of which is controlled by the derivative discontinuity. Third, because optimal tuning eliminates this error, the auxiliary orbital gap matches the interacting gap at low temperature, upgrading optimal tuning from a ground-state strategy to the governing principle -- mandatory, not optional -- for accurate finite-temperature gap predictions obtained from gaps of orbital eigenvalues within a hybrid functional framework. We present applications that validate the theory and demonstrate its consequences.

AI.tldr: This paper extends hybrid DFT to finite temperatures via a Mermin generalized Kohn-Sham framework, uses an extended Janak's theorem to derive a thermal orbital gap estimator, and shows that optimal tuning of the hybrid functional yields accurate finite-temperature fundamental gaps by eliminating derivative discontinuity errors.
AI.motivation: Predicting electronic fundamental gaps at finite temperature has remained conceptually and practically challenging, and no rigorous framework existed to address this.
AI.method: (1) Extending generalized Kohn-Sham hybrid DFT to thermal ensembles via a Mermin framework with a thermal one-particle auxiliary system. (2) Extending Janak's theorem to derive a thermal orbital gap estimator (thermal-quasiparticle picture) with a closed low-temperature form whose error is controlled by the derivative discontinuity. (3) Using optimal tuning to eliminate this error, making the auxiliary orbital gap match the interacting gap at low temperature.
AI.result: Optimal tuning upgrades from a ground-state strategy to a mandatory principle for accurate finite-temperature gap predictions from orbital eigenvalues within hybrid DFT.
AI.conclusion: Validated by applications, the theory establishes that optimal tuning is not optional but required for accurate finite-temperature gap predictions in hybrid functional frameworks.

title: Probing Light-Matter Interaction with Topological Data Analysis
summary: We explore application of Topological Data Analysis to study light matter interaction through scattering response data in different dimensions. This method is robust against Fano resonance backgrounds in both strong and weak coupling regimes, maintaining accuracy even with reduced mode contrast, distorted lineshape, and the introduction of random trace noise. It scales to any number of interacting modes, reflecting the system's effective degrees of freedom. Crucially, TDA is not merely peak counting but reveals phase-encoded features in the scattering response and may be used even for a fully saturated amplitude response. The analysis is also applied to a three mode system with time reversal symmetry breaking, revealing change in apparent number of loops and voids in combined two way scattering data. This approach is demonstrated to differentiate the three Dyson ensembles through their topological complexity and probability density functions, enabling analysis of complex modal systems.

AI.tldr: Topological Data Analysis (TDA) is applied to scattering response data across dimensions, showing robustness against Fano resonance backgrounds, noise, and reduced mode contrast. It reveals phase-encoded features beyond peak counting, scales to multiple interacting modes, and differentiates Dyson ensembles through topological complexity.
AI.motivation: To develop a robust method for analyzing light-matter interaction in scattering data that works despite challenging conditions like Fano resonance backgrounds, distorted lineshapes, noise, and reduced mode contrast, while going beyond simple peak counting.
AI.method: Topological Data Analysis is applied to scattering response data across dimensions, examining its performance in strong/weak coupling regimes, with random noise, and in multi-mode systems with time-reversal symmetry breaking. Three Dyson ensembles are differentiated through topological complexity and probability density functions.
AI.result: TDA maintains accuracy under adverse conditions (reduced contrast, distorted lineshapes, noise), scales to any number of interacting modes, reveals phase-encoded features even in fully saturated amplitude responses, and can detect changes in topological features (loops, voids) in multi-mode systems with broken time-reversal symmetry.
AI.conclusion: Topological Data Analysis provides a powerful, noise-robust framework for analyzing complex modal systems in light-matter interaction, capable of extracting phase-encoded information and distinguishing universal symmetry classes (Dyson ensembles) beyond what conventional peak-counting methods offer.

title: How is Water released in Hydrogen-Based Metal Oxide Reduction? Unraveling the Kinetic Bottleneck in Sustainable Metal Production
summary: Hydrogen-based direct reduction of metal oxides is a ubiquitous solid-gas redox process central to geophysics, sustainable metallurgy, redox energy cycles and catalysis. During this process, hydrogen removes lattice oxygen to form water, yet product water has long been regarded as a passive exhaust, and its nanoscale formation, trapping and removal remain poorly understood. Here, we directly observe redox-product water release from iron oxide during hydrogen-based direct reduction. Because water removal emerges from coupled structural, chemical and crystallographic evolution across multiple length-scales under realistic non-equilibrium reaction-conditions, we establish a correlative multiscale in-situ approach that links pore evolution, molecular water signatures, phase transformation and chemical-state evolution during hematite reduction. We uncover a mechanism in which oxygen removal induces closed nanopores spatially delocalized from reaction surfaces, causing transient trapping of water vapor. Water is released only when these pores coalesce into a percolating network connected to the surface, coinciding with and accelerating the onset of the hematite-to-magnetite transformation. These findings show that dynamically evolving pore topology governs mass transport and redox kinetics in solid-gas reactions, closing a critical mechanistic gap in product-water removal and providing nanoscale guidance for hydrogen-based metal extraction, reactor design, and sustainable redox energy technologies under practical conditions.

AI.tldr: This paper reveals that water product during hydrogen-based reduction of iron oxide is not a passive exhaust; it becomes transiently trapped in closed nanopores and is only released when pores coalesce into a percolating network. This pore-topology-governed mechanism dictates mass transport, reaction kinetics, and the onset of phase transformation (hematite-to-magnetite).
AI.motivation: Product water from hydrogen-based reduction of metal oxides has long been assumed a passive exhaust, but its nanoscale formation, trapping, and removal dynamics remain poorly understood, limiting progress in sustainable metallurgy, redox energy cycles, and catalysis.
AI.method: A correlative multiscale in-situ approach linking pore evolution, molecular water signatures, phase transformation, and chemical-state evolution during hematite reduction under realistic non-equilibrium reaction conditions.
AI.result: Oxygen removal induces closed nanopores spatially delocalized from reaction surfaces, causing transient water vapor trapping; water is released only upon pore coalescence into a percolating network connected to the surface, which coincides with and accelerates the hematite-to-magnetite transformation.
AI.conclusion: Dynamically evolving pore topology governs mass transport and redox kinetics in solid-gas reactions, closing a critical mechanistic gap in product-water removal and providing nanoscale guidance for hydrogen-based metal extraction, reactor design, and sustainable redox technologies.

title: Monotonic Impurity Entropy beyond Unitarity: the $\mathscr{PT}-$Symmetric Quantum Impurity Model
summary: Quantum impurity models provide a paradigmatic setting for studying Kondo screening, boundary criticality, and impurity entropies. While these phenomena are well understood in unitary systems, their fate in non-Hermitian many-body settings remains largely unexplored. We study a $\mathscr{PT}$-symmetric quantum impurity model consisting of a unitary $SU(2)_1$ Wess--Zumino--Witten bulk coupled to two impurity spins through complex-conjugate boundary Kondo interactions. Using an integrable lattice realization with $\mathscr{PT}$-symmetric boundary impurities, solved by the Bethe Ansatz and benchmarked against finite-temperature matrix-product-state calculations, we determine the impurity contribution to the free energy and entropy. In the Kondo-screened regime, where the spectrum remains entirely real and the impurities are screened by many-body Kondo clouds, we find that the impurity entropy decreases monotonically from $\ln 4$ in the ultraviolet to $0$ in the infrared. This monotonic flow persists despite the nonunitary nature of the boundary interaction, which places the system beyond the standard assumptions of the $g$-theorem.

AI.tldr: A $\mathscr{PT}$-symmetric quantum impurity model with unitary $SU(2)_1$ WZW bulk and complex-conjugate Kondo boundary couplings is studied via integrable lattice realization, Bethe Ansatz, and MPS calculations. The impurity entropy flows monotonically from $\ln 4$ to $0$ in the Kondo-screened regime, despite violating the standard $g$-theorem assumptions due to non-Hermiticity.
AI.motivation: To explore Kondo screening, boundary criticality, and impurity entropies in non-Hermitian many-body settings, which remain largely unexplored compared to unitary systems.
AI.method: Study a $\mathscr{PT}$-symmetric quantum impurity model with a unitary $SU(2)_1$ Wess-Zumino-Witten bulk coupled to two impurity spins via complex-conjugate boundary Kondo interactions. Use an integrable lattice realization with $\mathscr{PT}$-symmetric boundary impurities, solved by Bethe Ansatz, and benchmarked against finite-temperature matrix-product-state (MPS) calculations.
AI.result: In the Kondo-screened regime (purely real spectrum, impurities screened by many-body Kondo clouds), the impurity entropy decreases monotonically from $\ln 4$ in the ultraviolet to $0$ in the infrared.
AI.conclusion: Non-Hermitian $\mathscr{PT}$-symmetric boundary interactions can still exhibit monotonic impurity entropy flow despite violating the standard $g$-theorem assumptions, suggesting the possibility of a generalized $g$-theorem for non-Hermitian systems.

title: Spectral phase transitions and trainability in neural network learning dynamics
summary: The emergence of low-dimensional structures in the spectra of neural network weight matrices is a common empirical feature of trained models, but the dynamical origin of this phenomenon during learning remains an open problem. We formulate neural network training as the stochastic evolution of an initially random matrix ensemble, driven by stochastic gradient descent (SGD) updates that reshape the spectral bulk while amplifying signal strength. This induces a Baik-Ben Arous-Péché (BBP) transition during training, where isolated eigenvalues detach from the random bulk distribution, providing a dynamical framework for representation formation in high-dimensional learning dynamics. We demonstrate this in a solvable linear teacher-student model, where spectral evolution is analytically tractable and a phase diagram of trainability governed by the step size (or learning rate) and initial weight variance is obtained, and subsequently extend our formalism beyond the linear regime to nonlinear and stochastic settings. Numerical simulations in realistic settings support this picture, showing robust emergence of spectral alignment during training. Our results suggest that spectral analysis may provide a unified perspective of stochastic learning dynamics, linking trainability, optimisation hyperparameters, spectral phase transitions, and representation learning in neural networks.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that neural network training via SGD induces a BBP phase transition in the weight matrix spectrum, where isolated eigenvalues detach from the random bulk, explaining representation formation. This is analytically solved in a linear teacher-student model, yielding a phase diagram of trainability governed by learning rate and initial weight variance, and extended to nonlinear settings with numerical validation.
AI.motivation: Low-dimensional spectral structures in trained neural network weight matrices are commonly observed, but the dynamical origin of this phenomenon during learning remains an open problem.
AI.method: The paper formulates training as stochastic evolution of a random matrix ensemble under SGD, analytically studies a solvable linear teacher-student model to derive spectral evolution and trainability phase diagram, and extends the formalism to nonlinear and stochastic settings with numerical simulations.
AI.result: A Baik-Ben Arous-Péché (BBP) transition occurs during training, where eigenvalues detach from the random bulk. A phase diagram of trainability governed by step size (learning rate) and initial weight variance is obtained. Numerical simulations confirm robust spectral alignment.
AI.conclusion: Spectral analysis can provide a unified perspective linking trainability, hyperparameters, spectral phase transitions, and representation learning in neural networks.

title: Radiation Damage of TF-1 and PbWO$_4$ Crystals with 20 MeV Electrons
summary:
We studied the radiation hardness of two types of crystals, lead glass TF-1 and lead tungstate PbWO$_4$, using a 20 MeV electron beam from the LUE-75 linear accelerator at AANL. The transmittance of the crystals in the wavelength range of 200-1000 nm was measured before and after irradiation, and after thermal annealing. %
The irradiation was performed in two stages. First, both crystals were irradiated with beam current of 0.125 $μ$A, each for a total exposure time of 720 s and absorbing $5.6 \times 10^{14}~e^-$. %
Strong degradation of the optical properties of TF-1 caused by this amount of radiation was observed, while the effect on PbWO$_4$ was negligible (it is a few tens of times radiation harder than TF-1). %
In the second stage, only the PbWO$_4$ crystal was exposed to radiation, with a beam current of 0.28 $μ$A and an exposure time of 1200 s, absorbing an additional $2.1 \times 10^{15}e^-$, still no notable effect. %
Thermal annealing was performed in the temperature range of 160 to 250$^\circ$C (isochronal) for 10-12 hours. The transmittance of the annealed crystals increased with the annealing temperature and time.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates the radiation hardness of lead glass TF-1 and lead tungstate PbWO₄ crystals under 20 MeV electron beam irradiation, finding PbWO₄ to be significantly more radiation-hard (tens of times) than TF-1, with thermal annealing (160-250°C) recovering transmittance.
AI.motivation: To evaluate and compare the radiation hardness of TF-1 and PbWO₄ crystals for potential applications in high-radiation environments such as particle detectors.
AI.method: Crystals were irradiated with 20 MeV electrons from a LUE-75 linear accelerator in two stages: first both crystals at 0.125 μA for 720 s (5.6×10¹⁴ e⁻), then only PbWO₄ at 0.28 μA for 1200 s (2.1×10¹⁵ e⁻). Transmittance (200-1000 nm) was measured before/after irradiation and after isochronal thermal annealing at 160-250°C for 10-12 hours.
AI.result: TF-1 showed strong optical degradation after 5.6×10¹⁴ e⁻ irradiation. PbWO₄ exhibited negligible degradation at both irradiation stages (total >2.6×10¹⁵ e⁻), demonstrating tens of times higher radiation hardness. Thermal annealing effectively increased transmittance proportionally to temperature and time.
AI.conclusion: PbWO₄ is significantly more radiation-hard than TF-1, making it suitable for high-radiation environments. Thermal annealing can restore radiation-induced optical damage in both crystals.

title: The Position Space Chern Number: A Topological Index for Chiral Magnetic Systems
summary: This paper introduces an index that categorizes the topology of insulating chiral magnetic systems. The position space Chern number, $C_R$ is distinct from its momentum space counterpart, $C_K$. A nonzero index guarantees the existence of topologically protected in-gap states that localize on the edge of local potential barriers in momentum space. The Chern-Simons effective field theory describing position space Chern insulators reveals a topologically quantized correlation between transverse force operators that describe the flow of quanta in momentum space. We demonstrate the existence of nonzero $C_R$ in systems hosting skyrmion magnetic phases and show how the index generalizes the classical concept of a skyrmion winding number. Lastly we investigate the competition between momentum space and position space topologies, and highlight an apparent obstruction to having systems with both $C_R \neq 0$ and $C_K \neq 0$.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a position space Chern number (C_R) for insulating chiral magnetic systems, distinct from the momentum space Chern number (C_K). Nonzero C_R guarantees topologically protected in-gap states localized on momentum-space potential barriers. The authors develop a Chern-Simons effective field theory, demonstrate C_R in skyrmion systems (generalizing the skyrmion winding number), and find an obstruction to systems having both C_R ≠ 0 and C_K ≠ 0.
AI.motivation: To develop a new topological index (position space Chern number) for categorizing insulating chiral magnetic systems that captures topological phenomena distinct from the conventional momentum space Chern number, and to explore the interplay between these two types of topology.
AI.method: The authors define a position space Chern number C_R, develop a Chern-Simons effective field theory describing position space Chern insulators, analyze the correlation between transverse force operators in momentum space, and examine the competition between momentum space and position space topologies.
AI.result: Nonzero C_R guarantees topologically protected in-gap states localized at momentum-space potential barriers. C_R exists in skyrmion magnetic phases and generalizes the classical skyrmion winding number. There is an apparent obstruction to systems simultaneously having both C_R ≠ 0 and C_K ≠ 0.
AI.conclusion: Position space Chern number provides a fundamentally new topological classification for chiral magnetic systems, with quantized correlations between force operators, and reveals a mutual exclusivity between position space and momentum space topological phases.

title: Size Effects in the Strong-Field Ionization and Dissociation Dynamics of (H$_2$O)$_n$ (n=1-4)
summary: The size-dependent strong-field ionization and dissociation dynamics of (H$_2$O)$_n$ (n=1-4) are investigated using real-time time-dependent density functional theory (RT-TDDFT) coupled to Ehrenfest molecular dynamics under a common few-cycle near-infrared laser pulse. It is found that the net ionization per monomer varies only weakly on cluster size, whereas the protonic and oxygen response is changed much more strongly once the cluster size grows beyond the dimer. In particular, H-ejection activity is observed to rise sharply from the dimer to the trimer/tetramer regime, while stable H-transfer is essentially absent in the dimer under the present criterion but becomes substantial in the trimer and is further amplified in the tetramer. Through timing analyses, it is shown that the dimer exhibits a weak and temporally broad response, whereas the larger clusters display a much stronger early-time protonic response concentrated within and immediately after the laser pulse window. By endpoint oxygen statistics, a systematic increase in dissociation propensity with cluster size is likewise shown. For a clean subset of direct two-body dimer breakup trajectories, the asymptotic kinetic energy release is estimated to be 4.47 $\pm$ 1.03 eV, in reasonably good agreement with the experimental value for the unprotonated two-body Coulomb-explosion channel. Overall, it is shown by the results that increasing water-cluster size primarily reshapes the strong-field response through proton-mediated and topology-level nuclear dynamics rather than through a large change in net ionization alone.

AI.tldr: Using RT-TDDFT/Ehrenfest dynamics, the study finds that (H₂O)ₙ (n=1-4) cluster size weakly affects per-monomer ionization but strongly alters protonic and oxygen dynamics: H-ejection and H-transfer increase sharply beyond the dimer, larger clusters show earlier and stronger protonic response, and dissociation propensity grows with cluster size. The dimer's two-body Coulomb-explosion energy release (4.47 ± 1.03 eV) matches experiment. The work concludes that size effects are dominated by proton-mediated nuclear dynamics rather than ionization changes.
AI.motivation: To understand how water cluster size influences strong-field ionization and dissociation dynamics beyond simple ionization yield changes.
AI.method: Real-time time-dependent density functional theory (RT-TDDFT) coupled to Ehrenfest molecular dynamics under a few-cycle near-infrared laser pulse.
AI.result: Net ionization per monomer varies weakly with cluster size; H-ejection rises sharply from dimer to trimer/tetramer; stable H-transfer is absent in dimer but substantial in trimer and amplified in tetramer; larger clusters exhibit stronger early-time protonic response; dissociation propensity increases systematically with size; dimer two-body breakup yields 4.47 ± 1.03 eV kinetic energy release.
AI.conclusion: Increasing water-cluster size primarily reshapes the strong-field response through proton-mediated and topology-level nuclear dynamics rather than through a large change in net ionization alone.

title: Low-energy positron scattering from metastable helium
summary: Low-energy positron scattering from singlet and triplet metastable He($1s2s$) is investigated using the $R$-matrix propagation method in hyperspherical coordinates. Elastic and positronium-formation cross sections are reported, and near-threshold resonance structures are analyzed in terms of eigenphase sums and the time-delay matrix. For the triplet target, the calculated cross sections are in agreement with available convergent-close-coupling results and display the expected threshold behavior. Beyond the known $S$-wave features, Feshbach resonance series in higher partial waves extending up to highly excited atomic thresholds are systematically identified. The time-delay matrix further uncovers hidden resonances that produce obvious structures in the positronium-formation cross sections.

AI.tldr: The paper uses the R-matrix propagation method in hyperspherical coordinates to study low-energy positron scattering from metastable He(1s2s) in singlet and triplet states, reporting elastic and positronium-formation cross sections, and analyzing near-threshold resonances via eigenphase sums and time-delay matrix, including identification of Feshbach resonance series in higher partial waves and hidden resonances revealed by the time-delay matrix.
AI.motivation: To investigate low-energy positron scattering from metastable helium and systematically identify resonance structures, especially near-threshold Feshbach resonances in higher partial waves that have been less explored.
AI.method: R-matrix propagation method in hyperspherical coordinates; analysis via eigenphase sums and time-delay matrix.
AI.result: Cross sections for triplet target agree with convergent-close-coupling results; Feshbach resonance series in higher partial waves extending to highly excited thresholds are systematically identified; time-delay matrix uncovers hidden resonances that produce structures in positronium-formation cross sections.
AI.conclusion: The time-delay matrix is a powerful tool for revealing hidden resonances not obvious in eigenphase sums, and the method successfully describes near-threshold dynamics and resonance spectra in positron-metastable helium scattering.

title: Unit-Circle Moment Closure
summary: Moment closure is a central problem in reduced descriptions of stochastic, kinetic, and quantum dynamics, where equations for low-order observables are coupled to an unresolved hierarchy of higher-order moments. Existing closures usually impose a prescribed form on the distribution or directly truncate the hierarchy, which can become inaccurate or unstable for strongly non-Gaussian states. Here we introduce unit-circle moment closure, which recasts the problem as analytic continuation. Raw moments are mapped to bounded unit-circle moments, whose unresolved tail is reconstructed by a Takagi-Prony procedure from the effective pole structure of a mapped generating function. The resulting continuation yields stable higher-order moments without assuming a fixed distributional ansatz. Illustrative static and dynamical examples demonstrate accurate reconstruction of non-Gaussian distributions and stable evolution of moment hierarchies. Our approach provides a general perspective for moment closure based on analytic structure rather than direct truncation.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces unit-circle moment closure, a method that recasts moment closure as an analytic continuation problem by mapping raw moments to bounded unit-circle moments and reconstructing the unresolved tail via a Takagi-Prony procedure based on the pole structure of a generating function, enabling stable and accurate closure without assuming a fixed distributional form.
AI.motivation: Existing moment closure methods impose prescribed distributional forms or directly truncate the hierarchy, leading to inaccuracy or instability for strongly non-Gaussian states in stochastic, kinetic, and quantum dynamics.
AI.method: The method maps raw moments to bounded unit-circle moments, then reconstructs the unresolved tail of the hierarchy using a Takagi-Prony procedure that extracts the effective pole structure of a mapped generating function, performing analytic continuation rather than truncation.
AI.result: Illustrative static and dynamical examples demonstrate accurate reconstruction of non-Gaussian distributions and stable evolution of moment hierarchies.
AI.conclusion: The approach provides a general perspective for moment closure based on analytic structure rather than direct truncation, offering a stable and accurate alternative for reduced descriptions of complex dynamics.

title: Comment on "Fundamental limit of phonon Tesla valve for heat rectification from first principles"
summary: Thermal rectification is a two-terminal property: the same device must carry different heat-current magnitudes when two reservoir temperatures are interchanged. In this Comment on Ref.~\cite{WuHu2026}, we ask whether the reported ratio $γ=R_{\mathrm{f}}/R_{\mathrm{b}}$ can represent such a two-terminal rectification ratio within the fixed-background linearized phonon Boltzmann transport equation (BTE) used in that work. We show that, for a passive two-terminal reservoir problem, any fixed linearized BTE whose scattering operator preserves a uniform equilibrium temperature shift, and whose boundary-value problem is well posed, gives equal forward and reverse resistance magnitudes. A direction-dependent response can still occur under a prescribed gradient-weighted source--sink protocol, but such a response should be distinguished from two-terminal thermal rectification.

AI.tldr: This Comment challenges the claim of thermal rectification in Ref. [WuHu2026], showing that within the fixed-background linearized phonon BTE with proper boundary conditions, forward and reverse thermal resistances are necessarily equal. The reported asymmetry arises from a gradient-weighted source-sink protocol, not true two-terminal rectification.
AI.motivation: To question whether the rectification ratio reported in Ref. [WuHu2026] truly represents a two-terminal thermal rectification property or is an artifact of the chosen computational protocol.
AI.method: The authors analyze the theoretical framework of the linearized phonon Boltzmann transport equation (BTE) and demonstrate that for a passive two-terminal reservoir problem, any fixed linearized BTE with a scattering operator preserving uniform equilibrium temperature shifts yields equal forward and reverse resistance magnitudes. They distinguish this from a direction-dependent response under a prescribed gradient-weighted source-sink protocol.
AI.result: Forward and reverse resistance magnitudes are equal under the proper two-terminal reservoir boundary conditions in the linearized BTE framework. The reported asymmetry in Ref. [WuHu2026] stems from a different (source-sink) protocol.
AI.conclusion: The claimed rectification ratio in Ref. [WuHu2026] does not represent genuine two-terminal thermal rectification within the linearized BTE formalism used, but rather reflects a protocol-dependent directional asymmetry that should be classified separately.

title: The Squealer: Sensification of model exploration and model misfit
comment: 18 pages, 11 figures. Submitted to the Journal of Computational and Graphical Statistics
summary: We introduce a method for visual and auditory feedback when exploring the fit of a model to data. Starting with a best-fit curve fit to data, the user can drag the curve to a new position and the computer will emit a squeal, becoming louder and more unpleasant as the discrepancy between curve and data increases. We demonstrate with four examples: a two-parameter curve fit to golf putting data, a four-parameter curve fit to dilution assays, a fit to cosmological data sensitive to the parameters of the Big Bang model, and a nonparametric Gaussian process fit to temperature readings.

AI.tldr: Introduces a method providing visual and auditory feedback for exploring model-data fit, where dragging a fitted curve produces an unpleasant squeal that intensifies with increasing discrepancy; demonstrated on four diverse examples.
AI.motivation: To create an intuitive, multimodal (visual+auditory) interface for users to explore and understand how well a model fits data, leveraging sound to communicate misfit intensity.
AI.method: A user-draggable curve system that computes discrepancy between the dragged curve and data points, mapping this error to an auditory squeal whose loudness and unpleasantness increase with misfit.
AI.result: Demonstrated on four examples: golf putting (2-param), dilution assays (4-param), Big Bang cosmology parameters, and Gaussian process temperature fits.
AI.conclusion: The auditory feedback provides an additional perceptual channel for assessing goodness-of-fit, making model-data discrepancy more immediate and intuitive.

title: Distinct Roles of Hydrogen in Superconducting and Ferromagnetic Phases of CoZr$_{2}$H$_{x}$
summary: Hydrogenation offers a versatile route to tuning the physical properties of intermetallic compounds. In this study, we synthesized CoZr$_{2}$H$_{x}$ with different hydrogen contents and found that hydrogen is incorporated in two distinct concentration regimes separated by a wide composition gap: a low-concentration hydrogenated superconducting phase ($x$ = 0-0.054) and a high-concentration hydrogenated ferromagnetic phase ($x$ = 2.786). Hydrogen plays fundamentally different roles in the two concentration regimes. In the high hydrogen concentration phase, the Zr-H interactions substantially modify the metallic bands crossing the Fermi level, leading to the emergence of ferromagnetism. In contrast, in the low hydrogen concentration phase, hydrogen behaves as a nonmagnetic impurity without altering the electronic band structure. Despite the nearly identical Debye temperatures across the low-concentration series, the superconducting transition temperature ($T_{\mathrm{c}}$) is progressively suppressed with increasing hydrogen content.The observed $T_{\mathrm{c}}$ suppression is quantitatively described by the Abrikosov-Gor'kov pair-breaking theory, indicating that the superconducting gap of CoZr$_{2}$ is anisotropic or multigap rather than a fully isotropic $s$-wave symmetry.

AI.tldr: Hydrogenation of CoZr₂ creates two distinct phases: a low-concentration superconducting phase (x=0-0.054) where H acts as a nonmagnetic impurity that suppresses Tc via pair-breaking, and a high-concentration ferromagnetic phase (x=2.786) where Zr-H interactions modify band structure to induce ferromagnetism. Tc suppression follows Abrikosov-Gor'kov theory, suggesting anisotropic or multigap superconductivity.
AI.motivation: To understand how hydrogen incorporation tunes the physical properties of the intermetallic compound CoZr₂, particularly the emergence of distinct electronic phases and the nature of its superconducting gap symmetry.
AI.method: Synthesis of CoZr₂Hₓ with varying hydrogen content, characterization of two concentration regimes (low and high), measurement of superconducting transition temperature, and analysis of Tc suppression using Abrikosov-Gor'kov pair-breaking theory.
AI.result: Two distinct hydrogen concentration regimes exist with a wide composition gap: a low-concentration superconducting phase (x=0-0.054) and a high-concentration ferromagnetic phase (x=2.786). In the low-concentration regime, Tc is progressively suppressed without changes to Debye temperature or band structure, quantitatively described by Abrikosov-Gor'kov theory.
AI.conclusion: CoZr₂ exhibits anisotropic or multigap superconductivity rather than fully isotropic s-wave symmetry, as inferred from the pair-breaking behavior. Hydrogen serves as a nonmagnetic impurity at low concentrations but fundamentally alters electronic structure at high concentrations to induce ferromagnetism.

title: Decision-support strategies for photovoltaic self-consumption under declining electricity prices and limited remuneration of surplus generation
summary:
The success of distributed photovoltaics may be undermining its own future. As solar penetration increases, electricity prices decline during periods of peak generation, reducing the value of surplus photovoltaic production. This raises a critical question: can citizen-led energy systems remain economically viable in electricity markets dominated by renewable generation?
  Rather than exploring technically optimal but institutionally unrealistic solutions, we examine the options available under current regulatory and market conditions. Using high-resolution consumption data from a rural community sharing a PV facility among 24 users, we identify pathways for long-term sustainability. The study makes two contributions. First, it shows that effective internal coordination can mobilize participation and investment as successfully as external subsidies. Second, it compares static, dynamic, and hybrid energy-sharing models, with and without storage, providing a flexible framework that balances efficiency, fairness, and governance.
  Results show that collective self-consumption reduces required PV capacity, lowers investment costs, and increases annual savings compared with individually operated systems. Alternative allocation schemes further improve benefit distribution and local electricity use, although gains depend on trade-offs between efficiency, fairness, and governance complexity. Under current electricity prices and remuneration schemes, battery storage provides limited additional economic value and becomes attractive only under specific market conditions. Overall, the long-term viability of citizen-led photovoltaic initiatives depends less on technological sophistication than on collective coordination and adaptive governance.

AI.tldr: This paper examines the economic viability of citizen-led solar energy systems under high renewable penetration, showing that collective self-consumption with effective internal coordination can outperform individually operated systems, while battery storage offers limited value under current market conditions.
AI.motivation: The success of distributed photovoltaics may undermine itself as high solar penetration reduces electricity prices during peak generation periods, threatening the economic viability of citizen-led energy systems in renewable-dominated markets.
AI.method: Using high-resolution consumption data from a rural community of 24 users sharing a PV facility, the study compares static, dynamic, and hybrid energy-sharing models with and without storage, analyzing pathways under current regulatory and market conditions.
AI.result: Collective self-consumption reduces required PV capacity, lowers investment costs, and increases annual savings compared to individual systems. Alternative allocation schemes improve benefit distribution and local electricity use. Battery storage provides limited additional economic value and is attractive only under specific market conditions.
AI.conclusion: The long-term viability of citizen-led photovoltaic initiatives depends less on technological sophistication than on collective coordination and adaptive governance. Effective internal coordination can mobilize participation and investment as successfully as external subsidies.

title: Vortex-enhanced photovoltaic current in disordered topological materials
summary: In disordered topological materials, real-space crystalline defects interplay with momentum-space wave function singularities to \textit{enhance} the bulk photovoltaic current. What's singular is the interband Berry phase, or equivalently the phase of the \textit{optical} dipole matrix element, which has a \textit{vortex} structure in momentum space. Such \textit{optical vorticity} is guaranteed to exist in all topological materials associated with nontrivial Chern numbers. These vortices enhance electron-impurity skew scattering, which manifests as a ballistic photovoltaic current that is sensitive to (a) the topological material class, (b) the symmetry class of crystalline defects, and (c) the light polarization. This sensitivity manifests in two ways: firstly, by (a-c)-dependent frequency exponents for the photovoltaic current $\propto ω^{\text{exponent}}$ in topological semimetals, with $ω$ the frequency of the light source. Secondly, by (a-c)-dependent constraints of the bulk photovoltaic tensor, which are explainable only by emergent, \textit{magnetic} symmetries of \textit{time-reversal-invariant} topological materials. These ideas are concretized by case studies on multifold fermions, 3D $m$-order Weyl semimetals and 2D $n$-order Dirac systems, which include $n$-layer rhombohedral graphene, transition metal dichalcogenides, and topological surface states. Theoretical guidance is provided for a tri-pronged experimental program that combines frequency-tuned photoconductivity measurements, defect characterization and defect engineering.

AI.tldr: In disordered topological materials, crystalline defects interact with momentum-space Berry phase singularities (optical vorticity) to enhance bulk photovoltaic currents. This enhancement depends on the topological material class, defect symmetry class, and light polarization, leading to distinct frequency exponents and photovoltaic tensor constraints. Case studies include multifold fermions, Weyl/Dirac semimetals, rhombohedral graphene, TMDs, and topological surface states.
AI.motivation: To understand how real-space crystalline defects and momentum-space wave function singularities (Berry phase vortices) cooperatively enhance the bulk photovoltaic effect in topological materials, and to provide a unified theoretical framework linking topological class, defect symmetry, and light polarization to photocurrent responses.
AI.method: The paper develops a theory of optical vorticity (vortex structure of the interband Berry phase / optical dipole matrix phase) in topological materials with nontrivial Chern numbers, and analyzes how these vortices enhance electron-impurity skew scattering, producing a ballistic photovoltaic current. The analysis is concretized through case studies on multifold fermions, 3D m-order Weyl semimetals, and 2D n-order Dirac systems.
AI.result: (1) Optical vorticity is guaranteed in all topological materials with nontrivial Chern numbers. (2) The photovoltaic current shows sensitivity to topological class, defect symmetry class, and light polarization. (3) This sensitivity yields (a-c)-dependent frequency exponents $\propto \omega^{\text{exponent}}$ in topological semimetals. (4) Emergent magnetic symmetries in time-reversal-invariant topological materials explain (a-c)-dependent constraints on the bulk photovoltaic tensor.
AI.conclusion: The work provides theoretical guidance for a tri-pronged experimental program combining frequency-tuned photoconductivity, defect characterization, and defect engineering to probe and harness these topological photovoltaic effects.

title: Geometric Approach to Zero-Memory Quantum Dot Reservoir Computing
summary: Physical reservoir computing offers an energy-efficient alternative to conventional neural networks, where the intrinsic memory capacity in the physical system plays a central role. We demonstrate that memory capacity can be engineered extrinsically in memoryless systems by exploiting the computational space-time tradeoff, substituting temporal memory with spatial degrees of freedom. Our approach utilizes multidimensional input nodes to function as a spatial memory axis, thereby removing the dependency on intrinsic history-dependent dynamics in the reservoir. We validate this framework through numerical simulations of a generalized quantum dot, whose discrete energy levels provide strong nonlinearity crucial for reservoir computing as well. By coupling this inherent nonlinearity with our extrinsic memory, we show that memoryless quantum reservoir can achieve high performance on both chaotic Mackey-Glass future prediction and nonlinear transformation tasks. Furthermore, by analyzing the geometry of the quantum state trajectories, we identify the physical mechanism underlying this memory emergence: extrinsic memory constructs a hysteresis loop within the quantum Hilbert space, and this loop becomes topologically stable when the evolution of the system state synchronizes with the input signal's frequency. Our work decouples reservoir computing from material-specific memory properties, significantly expanding the range of candidate systems for quantum neuromorphic computing.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates that memory capacity in physical reservoir computing can be engineered extrinsically using spatial degrees of freedom instead of relying on intrinsic temporal memory, validated through numerical simulations of a generalized quantum dot system where extrinsic memory constructs topologically stable hysteresis loops in the quantum Hilbert space.
AI.motivation: To decouple reservoir computing from material-specific memory properties and expand the range of candidate systems for quantum neuromorphic computing by replacing intrinsic temporal memory with extrinsic spatial memory.
AI.method: Leveraging the computational space-time tradeoff, multidimensional input nodes serve as a spatial memory axis. Validated via numerical simulations of a generalized quantum dot with discrete energy levels providing strong nonlinearity. Geometric analysis of quantum state trajectories identifies hysteresis loop formation as the physical mechanism.
AI.result: Memoryless quantum reservoir achieves high performance on chaotic Mackey-Glass future prediction and nonlinear transformation tasks. Extrinsic memory constructs a hysteresis loop in quantum Hilbert space that becomes topologically stable when system evolution synchronizes with input signal frequency.
AI.conclusion: Reservoir computing can be decoupled from intrinsic material memory properties, significantly broadening candidate systems for quantum neuromorphic computing.

title: mCGCNN: A Dual-Stream Crystal Graph Convolutional Neural Network for the Efficient Prediction of Magnetic Properties of Crystalline Materials
summary: Magnetic order in crystals is governed by moment-carrying sublattices and ligand-mediated exchange pathways, yet standard crystal graph neural networks treat all atoms homogeneously and encode bonds primarily through pair distances. We propose mCGCNN, a magnetism-aware crystal graph network that augments the full structural graph with a dedicated magnetic subgraph. The magnetic stream performs angle-aware message passing over magnetic centers using metal-ligand-metal exchange-path descriptors motivated by Goodenough-Kanamori-Anderson physics, while layer-wise cross-coupling transfers structural and ligand-field information from the full crystal graph. A separate magnetic-sublattice pooling operation prevents the magnetic interaction from being diluted by nonmagnetic atoms. Benchmarked on a curated Materials Project spin-polarized DFT data, mCGCNN improves total magnetic moment prediction from a CGCNN test MAE of 2.54~$μ_B$ to 2.02~$μ_B$, outperforming a strengthened CGCNN readout baseline and raising the test $R^2$ from 0.644 to 0.776. When pretrained on moment regression, the same magnetic representation improves ferromagnetic/antiferromagnetic classification. The results demonstrate that incorporating exchange geometry directly into graph architectures provides a physically grounded route to predictive models of magnetic materials.

AI.tldr: mCGCNN is a magnetism-aware crystal graph neural network that improves magnetic moment prediction by augmenting standard crystal graphs with a dedicated magnetic subgraph using metal-ligand-metal exchange-path descriptors based on Goodenough-Kanamori-Anderson physics, achieving significant accuracy gains over standard CGCNN.
AI.motivation: Standard crystal graph neural networks treat all atoms homogeneously and encode bonds primarily through pair distances, failing to capture the physics of magnetic order governed by moment-carrying sublattices and ligand-mediated exchange pathways.
AI.method: mCGCNN augments the full structural graph with a magnetic subgraph that performs angle-aware message passing over magnetic centers using metal-ligand-metal exchange-path descriptors motivated by Goodenough-Kanamori-Anderson physics, with layer-wise cross-coupling for structural and ligand-field information transfer and a magnetic-sublattice pooling operation to prevent dilution by nonmagnetic atoms.
AI.result: mCGCNN improves total magnetic moment prediction from CGCNN test MAE of 2.54 μB to 2.02 μB, raises test R² from 0.644 to 0.776, outperforms strengthened CGCNN readout baseline, and improves ferromagnetic/antiferromagnetic classification when pretrained on moment regression.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating exchange geometry directly into graph architectures provides a physically grounded route to predictive models of magnetic materials.

title: TetMaG-Guided Design and Operando Electron Holography Validation of Current-Induced Domain-Wall Motion in 3D Curved and Cornered Fe Nanobridges
summary: Three-dimensional (3D) magnetic nanostructures offer new opportunities for controlling domain-wall (DW) configurations beyond the limitations of planar systems, providing promising architectures. However, the realization of reliable 3D magnetic devices requires precise control of geometry-dependent DW behaviour and quantitative experimental validation of the resulting magnetic states. Here, we combine TetMaG micromagnetic simulations, focused electron beam induced deposition (FEBID), and off-axis electron holography to investigate the influence of curvature and corner geometries on DW behaviour in 3D magnetic nanobridges. TetMaG simulations predict fundamentally different magnetic properties for curved and cornered geometries. Cornered nanobridges act as preferential DW pinning sites, stabilizing localized magnetic configurations and enabling controlled switching between neighbouring pinning positions. While curved nanobridges promote gradual magnetization rotation, reduced pinning, and smoother DW motion. These optimized geometries were fabricated with high structural fidelity using FEBID and subsequently characterized by quantitative electron holography. Electron holography measurements revealed magnetic induction maps that matched the simulated magnetization configurations, providing direct experimental validation of the TetMaG predictions. Curved and cornered geometries exhibited distinct DW characteristics governed by their local structural features, demonstrating the critical role of geometry in tailoring magnetic behaviour in 3D systems. Operando current-biasing experiments further revealed current-induced DW motion, including the displacement of a tail-to-tail DW into a head-to-tail configuration within corner structures.

AI.tldr: This paper combines simulations (TetMaG), nanofabrication (FEBID), and electron holography to study how curvature vs. corner geometry affects domain-wall behavior in 3D magnetic nanobridges, demonstrating geometry-controllable pinning and current-driven DW motion.
AI.motivation: Precise control of domain-wall behavior in 3D magnetic nanostructures is essential for reliable device operation, but quantitative experimental validation of geometry-dependent DW dynamics remains lacking.
AI.method: TetMaG micromagnetic simulations for predicting DW behavior; focused electron beam induced deposition (FEBID) for fabricating curved and cornered nanobridges; off-axis electron holography for quantitative magnetic induction mapping; operando current-biasing for DW motion experiments.
AI.result: Cornered nanobridges exhibit strong DW pinning and controlled switching between pinning sites; curved nanobridges show gradual magnetization rotation and reduced pinning. Electron holography directly validated simulations. Current-biasing induced DW displacement, including tail-to-tail to head-to-tail transitions in corner structures.
AI.conclusion: Geometry critically determines DW behavior in 3D magnetic nanostructures, with corners enabling pinning and switching control while curvature promotes smoother motion, validated quantitatively by experiment.

title: Low-lying $D$ states in yttrium and actinium ions highly sensitive to variation of the fine structure constant
summary: Whether fundamental constants vary over time or space is one of the key questions in metrology and cosmology. Among them, variation of the fine structure constant $α$ is intensively investigated. Yttrium ions Y$^+$ and actinium ions Ac$^+$ have low-lying $D$ states that are suitable for this search, with a proper path for laser cooling and detection. Theoretical calculations show that the sensitivities of the transitions between the ground state and the lowest $^3D_1$ states are $K=9.40$ and $K=9.73$, respectively. By driving the transition between the ground state and the $^3D_1$ states with a two-photon transition, the transition can be used for a high-sensitivity search for time variation of the fine structure constant. The high efficiency of a detection scheme using the transition between the $7s6d~^3D_1$ states and the $7s7p~^3P_0$ state also suggests that Ac$^+$ ions are potentially useful as a platform for quantum information processing.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates the potential use of Y⁺ and Ac⁺ ions for detecting temporal or spatial variation of the fine structure constant α, leveraging their low-lying D states with high sensitivity coefficients (K=9.40 for Y⁺, K=9.73 for Ac⁺), and also highlights Ac⁺ as a promising platform for quantum information processing due to efficient detection schemes.
AI.motivation: The fundamental question of whether constants like the fine structure constant α vary over time or space drives the need for high-sensitivity atomic transition probes in metrology and cosmology.
AI.method: Theoretical calculations of sensitivity coefficients K for ground state to lowest ³D₁ transitions in Y⁺ and Ac⁺, using two-photon transition schemes and detection via ³D₁ to ³P₀ transitions.
AI.result: Sensitivity coefficients K=9.40 for Y⁺ and K=9.73 for Ac⁺; high detection efficiency demonstrated for Ac⁺ using the 7s6d ³D₁ to 7s7p ³P₀ transition.
AI.conclusion: Both Y⁺ and Ac⁺ ions are suitable for high-sensitivity searches for α variation, and Ac⁺ additionally shows potential as a platform for quantum information processing.

title: Latent Genetic Algorithm for Crystal Structure Prediction
summary: Predicting crystal structures requires navigating rugged energy landscapes in which favorable local motifs must be inherited across candidates with incompatible cells, densities, and symmetries. Conventional real-space crossover often destroys these motifs when parent structures are geometrically mismatched. Here we show that latent representations learned by pretrained universal interatomic potentials can serve as continuous evolutionary coordinates for crystal structure prediction. In the Latent Genetic Algorithm (LGA), offspring are generated by inverse optimization of atomic positions and lattice vectors to match a target latent representation, which is constructed via interpolation of the parent latent vectors. LGA suppresses high-energy and short-contact offspring, increases the HfO$_2$ ground-state recovery rate from 20-35% to 60-95%, and enables a unified variable-supercell search over 16 perovskites with a nearly tenfold reduction in search cost. Applied to (PbTiO$_3$)$_n$/(PbZrO$_3$)$_n$ superlattices, LGA reveals $\sqrt{2} \times 3\sqrt{2} \times 1$ long-period ground-state structures characterized by a common in-plane finite-$q$ modulation $q{_\parallel} = (1/6,1/6)$ and layer-coupled sidebands. To our knowledge, this in-plane periodicity has not been reported in any related oxide perovskite superlattice studies. Altogether, LGA offers a powerful representation-guided paradigm for ground-state structure prediction and provides a practical, decoder-free route toward materials inverse design.

AI.tldr: LGA uses latent representations from pretrained interatomic potentials as evolutionary coordinates, enabling crystal structure prediction with 60-95% ground-state recovery (vs 20-35%), tenfold cost reduction for variable-supercell searches, and discovery of unreported long-period superlattice structures.
AI.motivation: Crystal structure prediction is challenged by rugged energy landscapes where favorable local motifs are destroyed during conventional real-space crossover due to geometric mismatches between parent cells, densities, and symmetries.
AI.method: Latent Genetic Algorithm (LGA): offspring are generated by inverse optimization of atomic positions and lattice vectors to match a target latent representation, constructed via interpolation of parent latent vectors from pretrained universal interatomic potentials, serving as continuous evolutionary coordinates.
AI.result: LGA suppresses high-energy/short-contact offspring, boosts HfO₂ ground-state recovery from 20-35% to 60-95%, achieves ~10× cost reduction in unified variable-supercell search across 16 perovskites, and discovers previously unreported √2×3√2×1 long-period ground-state structures in PbTiO₃/PbZrO₃ superlattices with in-plane modulation q∥=(1/6,1/6) and layer-coupled sidebands.
AI.conclusion: LGA offers a powerful representation-guided paradigm for ground-state structure prediction and provides a practical, decoder-free route toward materials inverse design.

title: Comparison of different exact generalized Langevin equations with a non-linear potential of mean force and an observable-dependent mass and friction
comment: 6 pages of main text including one figure
summary: The Mori-Zwanzig projection formalism constitutes a powerful and robust framework for deriving equations of motion in terms of generalized Langevin equations (GLEs) for an arbitrary observable using evolution and projection operators. Based on this framework, we analyze the properties of four distinct GLEs for a scalar observable including a Markovian force derived from a generally non-linear potential, a non-Markovian friction force, and an orthogonal force, commonly interpreted as a random force. While all four GLEs are exact, they differ in the memory friction kernel, which may either be dependent or independent of the observable, and by the potential, which may either include or exclude the effective kinetic energy of the observable. Inclusion of the kinetic energy in the potential is advantageous for observables whose velocity satisfies Wick's theorem, since this reproduces the correct distribution of the observable and its velocity even without contributions from the friction force and the orthogonal force.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes four exact Generalized Langevin Equations (GLEs) derived from the Mori-Zwanzig formalism for scalar observables, differing in memory friction kernel dependence and potential inclusion of kinetic energy. Including kinetic energy in the potential is advantageous when the observable's velocity follows Wick's theorem.
AI.motivation: To systematically analyze and compare four distinct GLE formulations derived from the Mori-Zwanzig projection formalism, clarifying their differences in memory friction kernels and potential terms, and identifying conditions under which specific formulations are advantageous.
AI.method: Theoretical analysis using the Mori-Zwanzig projection formalism with evolution and projection operators to derive four exact GLEs for a scalar observable, each differing in whether the memory friction kernel depends on the observable and whether the potential includes the effective kinetic energy.
AI.result: All four GLEs are exact but differ in their memory friction kernel (observable-dependent vs. independent) and potential (including vs. excluding effective kinetic energy). Including kinetic energy in the potential reproduces the correct distribution of the observable and its velocity without contributions from friction or orthogonal forces when the velocity satisfies Wick's theorem.
AI.conclusion: The formulation that includes kinetic energy in the potential is advantageous for observables whose velocity satisfies Wick's theorem, as it yields correct distributions even without explicit friction and orthogonal force contributions.

title: Anomalous Behavior of the Ni$^{1+}$ moment and interstitial band in bi-infinite-layered La$_3$Ni$_2$O$_5$F
summary: The discovery of superconductivity in hole-doped Ni$^{1+}$ systems with "infinite layer" NiO$_2$ square-lattices analogous to the Cu$^{2+}$ CaCuO$_2$ cuprate has renewed conflicting pictures of the Cu$^{2+}$$-$Ni$^{1+}$ similarity or distinction. Recent synthesis of formal Ni$^{1+}$ La$_3$Ni$_{2}$O$_{5}$F with two infinite NiO$_{2}$ layers per cell provides a novel member of this class. First principles density functional theory studies reveal an interstitial density derived single band $E^*$ in three layers unrelated to any atom, which provides self-doping to a Ni$^{1.09+}$ ion.The blocking La(O/F)La provides isolation of the NiO$_2$ bilayer and an interstitial $E^*$ density to strictly two-dimensional electronic and magnetic systems. Calculations of magnetic tendencies reveals behavior unlike previous nickelates, including vanishing susceptibility up to a large magnetic field. Two dimensional fluctuations and self-doping away from half-filling can account for the lack of observation of a magnetic transition.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates the electronic and magnetic properties of the newly synthesized infinite-layer nickelate La₃Ni₂O₅F, a Ni¹⁺ system analogous to cuprate superconductors. DFT calculations reveal an interstitial electron density (E*) layer that self-dopes the NiO₂ bilayers to Ni¹·⁰⁹⁺, creating a strictly 2D electronic/magnetic system with vanishing magnetic susceptibility up to high fields, attributed to 2D fluctuations and self-doping away from half-filling.
AI.motivation: To resolve conflicting views on the similarity or distinction between Cu²⁺ cuprates and Ni¹⁺ infinite-layer nickelates by studying a new member (La₃Ni₂O₅F) and understanding its electronic structure, self-doping behavior, and magnetic properties.
AI.method: First principles density functional theory (DFT) calculations were performed on La₃Ni₂O₅F to study its electronic structure, interstitial charge density, self-doping, and magnetic susceptibility tendencies.
AI.result: Discovered an interstitial-derived single band (E*) not associated with any atomic site, which provides self-doping to Ni¹·⁰⁹⁺. The blocking La(O/F)La layer isolates the NiO₂ bilayer, creating a strictly 2D system. Magnetic calculations show vanishing susceptibility up to large magnetic fields, unlike previous nickelates.
AI.conclusion: The absence of a magnetic transition in La₃Ni₂O₅F can be explained by two-dimensional fluctuations and self-doping away from half-filling, distinguishing this system from other nickelates and providing insight into the cuprate-nickelate analogy.

title: Microscopic and macroscopic characterization: MBE-grown versus sputter-deposited Au/Co/Au thin films for CISS and MIPAC effect studies
summary: Chirality-induced spin selectivity (CISS) enables spin-dependent transport at chiral molecule/Au(111) interfaces and is used in spintronics when combined with ferromagnetic thin films in spin-valve-type hybrids. However, the influence of substrate microstructure on CISS and the related magnetization induced by the proximity of adsorbed chiral molecules (MIPAC) effect is still not well understood. In this study, we compare the effects of the adsorption of L-chiral alpha-helical alanine-rich peptides on Au/Co/Au ferromagnetic thin films fabricated by molecular beam epitaxy (MBE) and magnetron sputtering. X-ray reflectivity and X-ray diffraction show sharper interfaces and a narrower Au(111) rocking-curve width for the MBE-grown sample. However, atomic force microscopy and scanning tunneling microscopy images reveal that both sample types have locally smooth Au(111) surface regions suitable for peptide adsorption, despite clear differences in larger-scale morphology. Microscopic scanning tunneling spectroscopy after peptide exposure yields similar magnetization-direction-dependent tunneling currents in both sample types, confirming a similar magnitude CISS effect on the molecular scale. In contrast, macroscopic magneto-optical Kerr effect hysteresis loops and effect microscopy reveals that only sputter-deposited samples show slight coercivity enhancements and a consistent reduction in domain wall velocity after peptide exposure. These results suggest that microscopic CISS signatures are robust for both sample types, whereas macroscopic MIPAC-type magnetic responses are more sensitive to the substrate microstructure.

AI.tldr: This study compares the adsorption of chiral peptides on Au/Co/Au thin films grown by MBE vs. magnetron sputtering, finding that microscopic CISS signatures are robust across both sample types, while macroscopic MIPAC magnetic responses (coercivity, domain wall velocity) are more sensitive to substrate microstructure and only appear in sputter-deposited samples.
AI.motivation: The influence of substrate microstructure on CISS and the MIPAC effect at chiral molecule/Au(111) interfaces is not well understood, motivating a systematic comparison between different film growth methods.
AI.method: Au/Co/Au ferromagnetic thin films were fabricated by MBE and magnetron sputtering. Characterized by XRR, XRD, AFM, STM, STS, and MOKE before and after adsorption of L-chiral alpha-helical alanine-rich peptides.
AI.result: MBE samples had sharper interfaces and narrower Au(111) rocking curves. Both sample types showed locally smooth Au(111) surfaces. STS showed similar CISS magnitude microscopically. Only sputtered samples showed coercivity enhancement and reduced domain wall velocity macroscopically after peptide exposure.
AI.conclusion: Microscopic CISS is robust to substrate microstructure, while macroscopic MIPAC-type magnetic responses are sensitive to substrate microstructure.

title: Surviving the Attack of the Clones
summary: We consider a population dynamics model in which each diffusing particle that hits a catalytic surface can split into two independent copies (clones). The particles of such a growing-in-size population search in parallel for a hidden partially reactive target to trigger a reaction event (e.g., a viral attack).
