We investigate the statistics of the fastest first-reaction time (FRT) among all the particles. We establish a nonlinear integral equation for the survival probability and then analyze the associated probability density of the FRT and its moments. Lower and upper bounds on the mean FRT are then deduced in terms of the system parameters (target reactivity, catalytic rate, diffusivity, etc.). Because autocatalytic replication can rapidly increase the number of searchers, it can substantially accelerate the diffusive search. We solve the nonlinear equations numerically in a basic geometric setting and reveal advantages and limitations on the autocatalytic search.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes a population dynamics model where diffusing particles split into copies upon hitting a catalytic surface, searching in parallel for a partially reactive target. It establishes integral equations for first-reaction time (FRT) statistics, derives bounds on the mean FRT, and numerically solves the model to show that autocatalytic replication can accelerate diffusive search but with inherent limitations.
AI.motivation: To understand how autocatalytic replication (particles splitting into clones upon hitting a catalytic surface) affects the statistics of the fastest first-reaction time among a growing population of diffusing searchers searching for a hidden partially reactive target (e.g., viral attack).
AI.method: A nonlinear integral equation is derived for the survival probability of the system. The probability density and moments of the first-reaction time (FRT) are analyzed analytically. Lower and upper bounds on the mean FRT are deduced as functions of system parameters (target reactivity, catalytic rate, diffusivity). The nonlinear equations are solved numerically in a basic geometric setting.
AI.result: Autocatalytic replication can substantially accelerate the diffusive search by rapidly increasing the number of searchers. Numerical solutions reveal both advantages and limitations of the autocatalytic search mechanism.
AI.conclusion: The autocatalytic replication strategy accelerates first-reaction times compared to standard diffusion, but there exist practical limitations on its efficiency, quantified by the derived bounds on mean FRT.

title: Mixed-spin Heisenberg ladders in a magnetic field
summary: In this work, we study alternating mixed-spin $(s,S)$ Heisenberg ladders in the magnetic field $h$ using density matrix renormalization group and linear spin-wave calculations. The $h$ \textit{versus} interchain coupling $J_\perp$ phase diagram for the $(1/2,1)$ case is investigated in detail. { In particular, we demonstrate the compatibility between the critical line estimates and magnetic ordering by analyzing chains with variable values of $J_\perp$ and of $h$ along the chain, $J_\perp$ and $h$ scans, and considering the usual case of chains with uniform couplings}. The magnetization plateau at 1/3 of saturation magnetization, 1/3 - plateau, is observed for $J_\perp>0$ and in a limited range for $J_\perp<0$. The critical Kosterlitz-Thouless transition point, where the 1/3 - plateau closes, is identified through a finite-size analysis of the transverse spin correlation functions.

AI.tldr: This paper studies alternating mixed-spin (s,S) Heisenberg ladders in magnetic fields, focusing on the (1/2,1) case. Using DMRG and linear spin-wave methods, the authors map out the h vs. J⊥ phase diagram, identify a 1/3 magnetization plateau, and determine the Kosterlitz-Thouless transition point where the plateau closes.
AI.motivation: To investigate the phase diagram and magnetic ordering of alternating mixed-spin Heisenberg ladders under magnetic fields, particularly focusing on the compatibility between critical line estimates and magnetic ordering.
AI.method: Density matrix renormalization group (DMRG) and linear spin-wave calculations; analyzing chains with variable J⊥ and h values along the chain; J⊥ and h scans; finite-size analysis of transverse spin correlation functions.
AI.result: Observed a magnetization plateau at 1/3 of saturation magnetization for J⊥>0 and in a limited range for J⊥<0. Identified the Kosterlitz-Thouless transition point where the 1/3-plateau closes.
AI.conclusion: The critical line estimates are compatible with magnetic ordering, and the 1/3-plateau exists asymmetrically for positive and negative interchain couplings, with its closure marked by a Kosterlitz-Thouless transition.

title: Estimating Free Energy Differences with Virtually Escorted Trajectories
summary: For a process in which a system is driven irreversibly from equilibrium state $A$ toward equilibrium state $B$, the free energy difference $ΔF = F_B-F_A$ can be estimated using the work fluctuation theorem $\langle e^{-W/T}\rangle = e^{-ΔF/T}$, where $W$ and $T$ denote work and temperature. The estimate often suffers from poor convergence with the number of trajectories used to calculate the average. Borrowing ideas from escorted free energy estimation, and from diffusion models of machine learning, we show how to construct infinitely many work-like quantities, $W_θ$, that satisfy $\langle e^{-W_θ/T}\rangle = e^{-ΔF/T}$, for the same underlying dynamics. Our method involves a virtual control field ${\boldsymbol u}_θ$ that does not modify these dynamics. We show how to choose parameter values $θ$ to optimize convergence of the free energy estimate, for a fixed set of trajectories. We identify conditions under which our method provides a zero-variance estimator of $ΔF$. We use numerical simulations of model systems to illustrate the gains in convergence that our method can achieve.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a method to construct infinitely many work-like quantities that satisfy the same fluctuation theorem as standard work, using a virtual control field that doesn't alter the underlying dynamics, enabling optimized convergence of free energy estimates and achieving zero-variance estimation under certain conditions.
AI.motivation: Free energy difference estimation via the work fluctuation theorem often suffers from poor convergence with the number of trajectories used in the average, motivating the need for improved estimators.
AI.method: The method borrows ideas from escorted free energy estimation and diffusion models to construct infinitely many work-like quantities W_θ that satisfy the same fluctuation theorem. It introduces a virtual control field u_θ that does not modify the underlying dynamics but allows optimization of convergence by tuning parameter values θ.
AI.result: The method can achieve zero-variance estimation of ΔF under identified conditions, and numerical simulations demonstrate significant gains in convergence compared to standard approaches.
AI.conclusion: The proposed approach provides a flexible framework for optimizing free energy estimates from a fixed set of trajectories, leveraging virtual control fields to improve convergence without altering the system dynamics.

title: Voltage-tunable Josephson Junctions on Germanium Quantum Wells with in-situ Aluminum Contacts
summary: Voltage-tunable Josephson junctions (VT-JJs) are an emerging element in superconducting quantum electronics with potential to expand the functionality of conventional designs. While VT-JJs are largely compatible with wafer-scale semiconductor processing, their integration into quantum circuits remains a challenge due to unmitigated semiconductor microwave loss. Here, a deep mesa etch process, wherein the epitaxial material is removed except the VT-JJ device, will facilitate the integration of VT-JJs with low-microwave-loss circuit elements by allowing these circuit elements to be placed directly on a low-loss substrate. A Germanium quantum well is grown by Molecular Beam Epitaxy (MBE) on a float zone silicon substrate with in-situ deposited aluminum contacts. This combination allows the formation of an oxide-free superconductor-semiconductor interface. The deep mesa etch process is optimized to produce a sidewall taper sufficient for continuous metal deposition from the substrate to the top of the mesa for electrostatic gate electrodes and interconnects. The fabricated Josephson junctions demonstrate gate-tunable supercurrents with a maximum critical current over 100 nA and critical-current normal-resistance product of $8.63~μV$. These results demonstrate a pathway toward improved integration of voltage-tunable superconducting circuit elements with quantum electronic building blocks such as couplers and qubits.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a deep mesa etch process for integrating voltage-tunable Josephson junctions (VT-JJs) with low-microwave-loss circuit elements on a low-loss substrate, using a Ge quantum well grown by MBE on float zone Si with in-situ Al contacts, achieving gate-tunable supercurrents over 100 nA and paving the way for improved quantum circuit integration.
AI.motivation: VT-JJs are promising for superconducting quantum electronics but suffer from unmitigated semiconductor microwave loss, hindering their integration into quantum circuits. The goal is to enable placement of low-loss circuit elements directly on a low-loss substrate while maintaining VT-JJ functionality.
AI.method: A deep mesa etch process removes epitaxial material except the VT-JJ device. A Ge quantum well is grown by MBE on a float zone Si substrate with in-situ deposited Al contacts, forming an oxide-free superconductor-semiconductor interface. The mesa etch is optimized to produce a sidewall taper for continuous metal deposition for gate electrodes and interconnects.
AI.result: Fabricated Josephson junctions show gate-tunable supercurrents with maximum critical current over 100 nA and a critical-current normal-resistance product of 8.63 μV.
AI.conclusion: The deep mesa etch approach offers a pathway toward improved integration of voltage-tunable superconducting circuit elements with quantum electronic building blocks such as couplers and qubits.

title: All-Optical Control of Birefringence in a Cold Atomic Ensemble
summary: We demonstrate all-optical control of birefringence in a cold atomic cloud of ytterbium. By optically dressing the excited $^{3}\mathrm{P}_1$ state via an off-resonant coupling to the $^{3}\mathrm{D}_1$ level, we induce polarization-dependent light shifts of the Zeeman sublevels, resulting in a tunable polarization-dependent refractive index. For a circularly polarized dressing beam, we observe a rotation of the probe linear polarization, characteristic of the Faraday effect, in the absence of any magnetic field. In addition, for a linearly polarized dressing beam, the probe acquires ellipticity without rotation, corresponding to linear birefringence. More generally, the polarization of the dressing beam controls the axis of rotation of the probe polarization on the Poincaré sphere. Our results establish cold atoms as a versatile platform for engineering and controlling light-induced birefringence and open new perspectives for the fast and reconfigurable control of optical response of resonant media.

AI.tldr: The authors demonstrate all-optical control of birefringence in a cold ytterbium atomic cloud by dressing the excited $^{3}\mathrm{P}_1$ state via off-resonant coupling to the $^{3}\mathrm{D}_1$ level, inducing tunable polarization-dependent refractive index. Circularly polarized dressing produces Faraday rotation (no magnetic field), linearly polarized dressing induces ellipticity without rotation, and the dressing beam polarization controls the probe polarization rotation axis on the Poincaré sphere.
AI.motivation: To achieve all-optical, fast, and reconfigurable control of birefringence in atomic media without external magnetic fields, using cold atoms as a versatile platform for engineering optical response.
AI.method: Optical dressing of the excited $^{3}\mathrm{P}_1$ state via an off-resonant coupling to the $^{3}\mathrm{D}_1$ level in a cold ytterbium atomic cloud, inducing polarization-dependent light shifts of Zeeman sublevels that produce a tunable polarization-dependent refractive index.
AI.result: Circularly polarized dressing beam causes probe linear polarization rotation (Faraday effect) without magnetic field; linearly polarized dressing beam induces probe ellipticity without rotation; the dressing beam polarization controls the axis of rotation of the probe polarization on the Poincaré sphere.
AI.conclusion: Cold atoms provide a versatile platform for engineering and controlling light-induced birefringence, enabling fast and reconfigurable control of optical response in resonant media.

title: Verified residual-specific explicit derivative kernels for physics-informed learning and discretized PDE adjoints
summary: Derivative computation is central to scientific computing, from space-time derivatives in physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) to residual Jacobian actions and discrete-adjoint operators in computational fluid dynamics (CFD). General-purpose automatic differentiation (AD) reduces implementation effort, but can incur substantial runtime and memory overhead for high-order residuals and complex discretized operators. Explicit derivative kernels can exploit problem-specific structure and provide efficient, controllable evaluations, but their use has been limited by derivation and implementation costs. This work revisits explicit differentiation (ED) as a residual-specific and verifiable route enabled by agent-assisted implementation and stringent numerical verification. For PINNs, we propose residual-specific partial-jet propagation, which makes the derivative-state closure of the target PDE residual explicit and realizes it through specialized layerwise kernels, rather than relying only on nested AD or a generic Taylor-mode transform. Relative to nested AD, the resulting ED kernels achieve floating-point-level agreement in residual and parameter-gradient evaluations and accelerate complete PINN training, often reaching 2-4x speedups while reducing peak GPU memory in most cases. For discretized PDE adjoints, we apply the same verification-driven strategy to a finite-volume CFD residual. The generated tangent-action and transpose-action kernels pass Taylor-remainder, inner-product, and reduced-gradient consistency checks, and are embedded into a GPU-resident discrete-adjoint workflow for freestream Mach-number and angle-of-attack inversion. These results suggest that verified explicit derivative kernels, supported by agent-assisted implementation, can serve as a practical, structure-aware complement to general-purpose AD for derivative-intensive scientific computing.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes explicit differentiation (ED) as a residual-specific, verifiable alternative to general-purpose automatic differentiation (AD) for derivative computation in scientific computing. Using agent-assisted implementation and numerical verification, ED kernels achieve 2-4x speedups in PINN training and enable efficient discrete-adjoint CFD workflows, demonstrating practical structure-aware complement to AD.
AI.motivation: General-purpose automatic differentiation (AD) incurs substantial runtime and memory overhead for high-order residuals and complex discretized operators. Explicit derivative kernels exploit problem-specific structure but have been limited by high derivation and implementation costs.
AI.method: Proposes residual-specific explicit differentiation (ED) enabled by agent-assisted implementation and stringent numerical verification. For PINNs, uses residual-specific partial-jet propagation with specialized layerwise kernels. For CFD, applies verification-driven strategy with Taylor-remainder, inner-product, and reduced-gradient consistency checks.
AI.result: ED kernels achieve floating-point-level agreement with nested AD in residual and parameter-gradient evaluations, accelerate PINN training 2-4x with reduced peak GPU memory. Generated tangent-action and transpose-action kernels pass consistency checks and are embedded into GPU-resident discrete-adjoint workflow for freestream Mach-number and angle-of-attack inversion.
AI.conclusion: Verified explicit derivative kernels, supported by agent-assisted implementation, can serve as a practical, structure-aware complement to general-purpose AD for derivative-intensive scientific computing.

title: Ultrafast directed transport via energy recuperation in non-Markovian systems
summary: A recent pioneering experiment [Nat. Commun. 16, 10114 (2025)] demonstrated that a driven overdamped colloidal particle in a harmonic trap immersed in a viscoelastic fluid can recuperate energy dissipated into the surrounding bath and convert it into useful work. In this article we considerably extend the original predictions. In particular, we show that energy recuperation is a generic feature of non-Markovian systems both in and out of equilibrium, even as simple as a free Brownian particle. Moreover, we demonstrate that inertia alone, even in the strong damping regime, can lead to this effect despite the absence of any external forcing. These results suggest that energy recuperation can be ubiquitous in nature and it may be the modus operandi of various phenomena in setups with memory. We show that this novel mechanism of energy recovery is the source of memory-induced ultrafast directed transport of a particle in a periodic potential in which it almost attains its top speed corresponding to the system with no energy barriers. Our results may answer from the fundamental point of view the question why the cytosol, the intracellular fluid in biological cells, is viscoelastic.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that energy recuperation (recovering dissipated energy as useful work) is a generic feature of non-Markovian systems with memory, occurring even in simple systems like a free Brownian particle or inertially-damped particles without external forcing. This mechanism enables ultrafast directed transport in periodic potentials and may explain why biological cytosol is viscoelastic.
AI.motivation: To extend previous experimental findings on energy recuperation in driven colloidal particles in viscoelastic fluids, and to demonstrate that this phenomenon is a generic feature of non-Markovian systems, not limited to specific experimental conditions.
AI.method: Theoretical analysis of non-Markovian systems (viscoelastic fluids with memory), examining energy recuperation in various configurations: free Brownian particles, inertially-damped particles without external forcing, and particles in periodic potentials.
AI.result: Energy recuperation is a generic feature of non-Markovian systems both in and out of equilibrium. It occurs even for a simple free Brownian particle and in the presence of inertia alone under strong damping without external forcing. This mechanism enables memory-induced ultrafast directed transport in periodic potentials, achieving speeds nearly matching barrier-free systems.
AI.conclusion: Energy recuperation may be ubiquitous in nature and could be the modus operandi for various phenomena in memory-containing setups. The results may fundamentally explain why cytosol in biological cells is viscoelastic.

title: Hydrostatic pressure effect on the pseudogap in Y0.77Pr0.23Ba2Cu3O7-δsingle crystals
summary: We studied the changes of resistivity $ρ(T)$, superconducting transition temperature $T_c$, fluctuation conductivity $σ'(T)$, and pseudogap $Δ^*(T)$ of $Y_{1-x}Pr_xBa_2Cu_3O_{7-δ}$ (YPrBCO) ($x = 0.23$) single crystal under hydrostatic pressure (HP) up to $\sim 1.1$ GPa. Defects created by magnetic inclusions of $PrBa_2Cu_3O_{7-δ}$ (PrBCO) were found to play a significant role in the behavior of the sample. The largest decrease in $ρ(T)$ was found depending on HP at a rate of $d\lnρ(100~K)/dP = -(29 \pm 0.2) \% \cdot GPa^{-1}$. This indicates that the mechanisms of the influence of HP on the $ρ(T)$ and $T_c$ of YPrBCO and $YBa_2Cu_3O_{7-δ}$ single crystals are different. From the analysis of the pseudogap, it was revealed that the mechanism of the interaction of charge carriers with magnetic PrBCO impurities changes three times with increasing HP. Relatively low HP, up to $\sim 0.5$ GPa, promotes the formation of defects caused by PrBCO magnetic inclusions. Starting from 0.6 GPa, the HP neutralizes the influence of magnetic impurities, and the magnetic maximum on $Δ^*(T)$ disappears. Above $\sim 1.0$ GPa, HP aligns the magnetic moments of PrBCO, and the magnetic maximum reappears on $Δ^*(T)$, more pronounced than at $P = 0$.

AI.tldr: This study investigates the effects of hydrostatic pressure (up to ~1.1 GPa) on resistivity, superconducting transition temperature, fluctuation conductivity, and pseudogap in YPrBCO single crystals (x=0.23), revealing pressure-dependent interactions with PrBCO magnetic impurities that change behavior at ~0.5 GPa and ~1.0 GPa thresholds.
AI.motivation: To understand how hydrostatic pressure influences the electronic transport properties and pseudogap behavior in YPrBCO single crystals, particularly the role of magnetic PrBCO inclusions and defects, and to reveal differences in pressure response compared to pure YBCO systems.
AI.method: Resistivity ρ(T), superconducting transition temperature Tc, fluctuation conductivity σ'(T), and pseudogap Δ*(T) of Y1-xPrxBa2Cu3O7-δ (x=0.23) single crystals were measured under hydrostatic pressure up to ~1.1 GPa.
AI.result: Resistivity decreases at dlnρ(100 K)/dP = -(29 ± 0.2)%·GPa⁻¹, indicating different pressure mechanisms from YBCO. Three pressure regimes identified: below ~0.5 GPa promotes PrBCO defect formation; ~0.6 GPa neutralizes magnetic impurity effects and suppresses the magnetic maximum in Δ*(T); above ~1.0 GPa aligns PrBCO magnetic moments, causing reappearance of a more pronounced magnetic maximum.
AI.conclusion: Hydrostatic pressure has a non-monotonic effect on the pseudogap and magnetic impurity interactions in YPrBCO, with distinct crossover pressures (~0.5 GPa and ~1.0 GPa) where the role of PrBCO magnetic inclusions fundamentally changes.

title: Multiphysical impedance spectroscopy of porous electrodes based on linear irreversible thermodynamics
summary: Porous electrodes couple electrical, chemical, mechanical, hydraulic, and thermal fields, yet conventional frequency-domain diagnostics interrogate only one of them: electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) the electrical response and dynamic mechanical analysis (DMA) the mechanical. Each reads a diagonal entry of the multiphysical constitutive matrix and is blind to the cross-couplings that govern structural evolution and degradation. Starting from linear irreversible thermodynamics, we formulate a general theory of multiphysical impedance spectroscopy, in which perturbing one field and measuring the conjugate response of another probes an off-diagonal entry of the constitutive matrix, recovering the static coupling coefficient and resolving its relaxation dynamics across frequency. Specializing to the electro-chemo-mechanical pathway yields a closed-form theory of mechano-electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (MEIS), in which a small harmonic current is applied and the stack stress is measured; the impedance factorizes into a chemical-accumulation term multiplying the sum of a chemo-mechanical and a poro-mechanical kernel. The porosity-accommodation bridge function is derived from a Helmholtz free energy -- following from a microstructural stiffness and viscosity rather than a fitted form -- and a three-phase (solid-fluid-void) closure interpolates continuously between unsaturated and Biot-saturated limits through a void-accommodation fraction. Non-dimensionalization reduces the spectrum to five groups, identifies the phase angle as the discriminator of the chemo-mechanical parameters, and locates the onset of second-quadrant behavior, which in a full cell arises from the competition between an expanding and a contracting electrode. MEIS emerges as one member of a family of cross-coupled spectroscopies the same framework brings within reach.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a general theory of multiphysical impedance spectroscopy that probes cross-couplings between fields (e.g., electro-chemo-mechanical) by perturbing one field and measuring the conjugate response of another, and specializes this to mechano-electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (MEIS) where a harmonic current is applied and stack stress is measured, yielding a closed-form theory with a porosity-accommodation bridge function derived from Helmholtz free energy and a three-phase solid-fluid-void closure.
AI.motivation: Conventional frequency-domain diagnostics (EIS, DMA) only interrogate single fields (electrical or mechanical) and are blind to the cross-couplings between multiphysical fields (electrical, chemical, mechanical, hydraulic, thermal) that govern structural evolution and degradation in porous electrodes.
AI.method: Starting from linear irreversible thermodynamics, the authors formulate a general theory of multiphysical impedance spectroscopy. Specializing to the electro-chemo-mechanical pathway yields MEIS: applying a small harmonic current and measuring stack stress. The impedance factorizes into a chemical-accumulation term times the sum of chemo-mechanical and poro-mechanical kernels. The porosity-accommodation bridge function is derived from Helmholtz free energy (microstructural stiffness and viscosity) with a three-phase (solid-fluid-void) closure interpolating between unsaturated and Biot-saturated limits via a void-accommodation fraction.
AI.result: Non-dimensionalization reduces the spectrum to five groups; the phase angle discriminates chemo-mechanical parameters; second-quadrant behavior onset is located, arising in a full cell from competition between expanding and contracting electrodes.
AI.conclusion: MEIS is one member of a family of cross-coupled spectroscopies that the same general framework can describe, enabling probing of off-diagonal entries of the multiphysical constitutive matrix.

title: Spontaneous Symmetry Breaking and Emergent Helicity in Achiral D4h-Symmetric Zinc Phthalocyanine Condensates
comment: 5 pages, 3 figures, Supplemental material included with 5 pages and 11 figures
summary: Herein it is shown spontaneous symmetry breaking in supramolecular aggregates of D4h-symmetric zinc phthalocyanine (ZnPc). Ab initio density functional theory calculations at the M06/DGDZVP level reveal that intermolecular interactions induce a subtle relaxation of the macrocyclic framework, producing a characteristic red shift of the aza-bridge (C-N-C) stretching mode and symmetric stretching of the pyrrole ring. Confocal Raman Optical Activity measurements further reveal a negative Cotton effect at 1505 cm^-1 and 1338 cm^-1, providing evidence of emergent supramolecular chirality. Our findings identify pristine ZnPc as a model system for spontaneous self-assembled chiral symmetry breaking in molecular condensates and suggest new opportunities for chiroptical, spin-selective, and quantum functional materials.

AI.tldr: Spontaneous symmetry breaking in D4h-symmetric ZnPc aggregates is demonstrated via DFT calculations and Raman Optical Activity, revealing emergent supramolecular chirality through red-shifted vibrational modes and a negative Cotton effect.
AI.motivation: To demonstrate spontaneous chiral symmetry breaking in pristine, achiral ZnPc supramolecular aggregates and establish it as a model system for self-assembled chiral materials.
AI.method: Ab initio DFT at M06/DGDZVP level for vibrational analysis; Confocal Raman Optical Activity (ROA) spectroscopy for chiroptical characterization.
AI.result: A red shift of the aza-bridge C-N-C stretching mode and pyrrole ring symmetric stretching; negative Cotton effect at 1505 cm⁻¹ and 1338 cm⁻¹ in ROA spectra.
AI.conclusion: Pristine ZnPc aggregates undergo spontaneous chiral symmetry breaking, opening avenues for chiroptical, spin-selective, and quantum functional materials.

title: Magnetic symmetry implications of the zero- and applied-field Hall effect of UNi$_4$B
summary: The zero-field and applied-field Hall effects in noncollinear antiferromagnets provide evidence for topological states of matter and are tied to materials' magnetic symmetry. For UNi$_4$B, the antiferromagnetic state with $T_\mathrm{N}=20$ K at zero and low magnetic field is debated due to recent magnetoelectric measurements and theory work calling into question the proposed toroidal arrangement of magnetic dipole moments. For a magnetic field applied within the plane of uranium magnetic moments, the field-dependent Hall resistivity of UNi$_4$B shows a curved response for $ρ_{yz}$ ($H{\parallel}x$, $I{\parallel}z$) and $ρ_{zx}$ ($H{\parallel}y$, $I{\parallel}x$) up to $\sim$8 T at 2 K, while an out-of-plane field results in linear behavior of $ρ_{yx}$ ($H{\parallel}z$, $I{\parallel}x$) up to 16 T. Analysis using conventional empirical relationships for the Hall effect indicate that an intrinsic effect from momentum-space Berry curvature contributes significantly to the curved transverse resistivity. Moreover, a finite zero-field Hall effect emerges at the onset of magnetic order for $ρ_{yz}$ and $ρ_{zx}$, further supporting an intrinsic origin of the Hall response. Symmetry arguments for a finite Berry curvature, an observable magnetoelectric effect, and reported magnetic structures suggest that the previously proposed magnetic space groups for the zero-field magnetic structure cannot account for the observed finite zero-field effect for two Hall orientations. Instead, we propose that $Cm'$ or $Pm'$ magnetic symmetry, depending on the parent nonmagnetic space group, is consistent with Hall resistivity, neutron diffraction, and magnetoelectric effect measurements.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates the Hall effect in the noncollinear antiferromagnet UNi$_4$B, finding curved Hall resistivity under in-plane fields and finite zero-field Hall effects, which indicate Berry-curvature-driven intrinsic contributions. The observed symmetries challenge the previously proposed toroidal magnetic structure and instead support $Cm'$ or $Pm'$ magnetic space groups.
AI.motivation: The magnetic structure of UNi$_4$B (antiferromagnetic below $T_N=20$ K) is debated because recent magnetoelectric and theoretical work questioned the proposed toroidal dipole arrangement. Resolving this is important for understanding topological states in noncollinear antiferromagnets.
AI.method: Field-dependent Hall resistivity measurements were performed for different orientations ($\rho_{yz}$, $\rho_{zx}$, $\rho_{yx}$) at 2 K up to 16 T. Data were analyzed using conventional empirical Hall-effect relationships to disentangle intrinsic (Berry curvature) from extrinsic contributions. Symmetry analysis was applied to the observed finite zero-field Hall effect and magnetoelectric response to constrain the magnetic space group.
AI.result: In-plane field ($H\parallel x,y$) produces curved $\rho_{yz}$ and $\rho_{zx}$ up to ~8 T, while out-of-plane field ($H\parallel z$) gives linear $\rho_{yx}$ up to 16 T. The curved response is attributed to an intrinsic Berry-curvature contribution. A finite zero-field Hall effect appears at $T_N$ for $\rho_{yz}$ and $\rho_{zx}$ but not for $\rho_{yx}$.
AI.conclusion: The previously proposed magnetic space groups cannot account for the two finite zero-field Hall orientations. The authors propose $Cm'$ or $Pm'$ magnetic symmetry as consistent with all experimental constraints (Hall resistivity, neutron diffraction, magnetoelectric effect).

title: NQS-Agent: Health-Aware Agentic Hyperparameter Optimization for Neural-Network Quantum States
summary: Neural-network quantum states (NQS) provide expressive variational representations for strongly correlated quantum many-body systems, but their practical accuracy depends sensitively on architecture-level hyperparameters and optimization schedules. Here we develop NQS-Agent, an implemented open-source software framework for health-aware hyperparameter optimization (HPO) in NQS calculations. Its workflow monitors energy trajectories, detects destructive optimization events, stops unstable calculations, modifies the learning-rate schedule, resumes optimization from safe checkpoints, and ranks candidates with an anomaly-aware score. We demonstrate the approach on a residual convolutional NQS for the square-lattice Heisenberg $J_1$-$J_2$ model, using architectures with parameter counts comparable to aCNN, a convolutional NQS architecture used here as a reference. The results show that NQS-Agent improves over the reported human-tuned aCNN baseline for the aCNN reference architecture and identifies a structurally distinct wide-and-shallow competitive candidate within the parameter-count-matched residual-CNN search space. These results show that the stability and recovery history of an optimization trajectory should be considered when assessing an NQS result. Health-aware HPO therefore provides a reproducible tuning protocol that goes beyond selecting a single lowest-energy calculation.

AI.tldr: NQS-Agent is an open-source framework for health-aware hyperparameter optimization in neural-network quantum state calculations that monitors optimization trajectories, detects instabilities, and ranks candidates beyond lowest-energy selection, demonstrating improvements on the square-lattice Heisenberg J1-J2 model.
AI.motivation: The accuracy of neural-network quantum states (NQS) is highly sensitive to architecture-level hyperparameters and optimization schedules, and there is a lack of automated, reproducible protocols for hyperparameter optimization in this domain.
AI.method: NQS-Agent implements a workflow that monitors energy trajectories, detects destructive optimization events, stops unstable calculations, modifies learning-rate schedules, resumes from safe checkpoints, and ranks candidates using an anomaly-aware score.
AI.result: NQS-Agent improves over the human-tuned aCNN baseline on the square-lattice Heisenberg J1-J2 model and identifies a structurally distinct wide-and-shallow competitive candidate within the parameter-count-matched residual-CNN search space.
AI.conclusion: Stability and recovery history of an optimization trajectory should be considered when assessing NQS results; health-aware HPO provides a reproducible tuning protocol beyond selecting the single lowest-energy calculation.

title: Surrogate-Gated Generation and Foundation-Model Embeddings for Bayesian Materials Design
summary: Closed-loop materials discovery iterates between proposing candidate structures and evaluating their properties, and property evaluation dominates the cost. In the generative variant, a learned prior proposes candidate crystals and a property oracle scores them; we ask whether a cheap probabilistic surrogate can triage the generator's output, and what such a surrogate must do well. Across three architecturally distinct pretrained diffusion priors (MatterGen, CrystalFlow, ADiT) and two targets (room-temperature heat capacity and bulk modulus), we insert a Gaussian process acquisition gate between structure generation and the oracle in an RL-steered generative workflow. The gate matches or exceeds ungated fine-tuning of the generative model while capping oracle calls at a fixed per-cycle budget. Budget-matched ablations isolate the mechanism. At an identical four-call budget, ranking-based selection outperforms arbitrary selection, confirming that the gain comes from the surrogate's choice; the gate comes within $\sim$9\% of exhaustive oracle spending at roughly one-fifth of the calls. A density-functional-theory check of the bulk-modulus discoveries confirms the learned oracle to within 2.5\% on average and the surrogate's ranking of the generated structures at Spearman $ρ= 0.94$. A cross-factorial benchmark of surrogate performance spanning mechanical, electronic, and vibrational properties identifies pretrained ORB embeddings with a Gaussian process as the most reliable combination, which we adopt as the building blocks of the proposed workflow. The complete pipeline is released as open-source software.

AI.tldr: A Gaussian process surrogate gating mechanism is inserted between structure generation and expensive property oracles in closed-loop materials discovery, matching or exceeding fine-tuned generative models while using ~80% fewer oracle calls, with ORB embeddings + GP as the most reliable surrogate combination.
AI.motivation: Property evaluation (oracle calls) dominates cost in closed-loop materials discovery. The authors ask whether a cheap probabilistic surrogate can triage generated candidate crystals before expensive evaluation, and what capabilities such a surrogate must possess to be effective.
AI.method: Insert a Gaussian process acquisition gate between three pretrained diffusion priors (MatterGen, CrystalFlow, ADiT) and a property oracle in an RL-steered generative workflow. Test on room-temperature heat capacity and bulk modulus. Use budget-matched ablations, ranking-based vs. arbitrary selection comparison, DFT verification, and cross-factorial benchmark of surrogate configurations.
AI.result: Gate matches/exceeds ungated fine-tuning while capping oracle calls per cycle. At 4-call budget, ranking-based selection outperforms arbitrary selection. Gate achieves ~9% of exhaustive oracle spending with ~1/5 the calls. DFT check shows ~2.5% average error and Spearman ρ=0.94 for surrogate ranking. ORB embeddings + GP is the most reliable surrogate combination.
AI.conclusion: A probabilistic surrogate gate can significantly reduce oracle costs in generative materials discovery while maintaining quality, with ranking capability being the key mechanism. ORB embeddings + Gaussian process is recommended as the surrogate building block. The pipeline is released as open-source.

title: Graphene as a Tunable Nonradiative Bath for Moiré Excitons
summary: A minimal theory for the nonradiative transfer of energy from a two-dimensional (2D) exciton -- especially a moiré-localized exciton -- to a nearby graphene layer is presented. Starting from Fermi's golden rule, the transfer rate is written as the overlap between the exciton near-field spectrum and the long-wavelength electronic loss function of graphene, weighted by an exciton form factor. In the point-dipole limit the framework reproduces the established $\GET\propto z^{-4}$ law for energy transfer to graphene. Including the finite spatial extent of a moiré exciton through a Gaussian form factor with localization length $\lX$, we show that high-momentum components of the near field are filtered out for $z\lesssim\lX$, so that the transfer rate -- and hence the photoluminescence (PL) quenching -- can serve as a probe of exciton localization. Treating graphene as a gate-tunable bath, a Pauli-blocking model predicts that interband electron-hole excitations are strongly suppressed once $2|\muF|$ approaches $\hbarω$, partially restoring PL intensity and lifetime. Benchmarking against the full random-phase-approximation loss function of doped graphene confirms the minimal model to within a few percent over the relevant distance range for representative near-infrared exciton parameters. We map the resulting PL observables over experimentally relevant ranges of spacer thickness, localization length, emission energy, and Fermi level, and identify when graphene-induced quenching dominates the optical response of transition-metal dichalcogenide/hexagonal boron nitride/graphene heterostructures. A graphene gate thus acts not as a passive electrostatic element but as a tunable 2D electronic reservoir whose long-wavelength response can be probed through exciton PL quenching.

AI.tldr: A minimal theory for nonradiative energy transfer from 2D/moiré excitons to graphene is developed, showing the transfer rate depends on exciton localization length and graphene's gate-tunable electronic response, enabling PL quenching as a probe of exciton properties and graphene's long-wavelength response.
AI.motivation: To understand and model nonradiative energy transfer from 2D excitons (especially moiré-localized excitons) to graphene, and to show that graphene's gate-tunable response can be used to probe exciton localization and control photoluminescence quenching.
AI.method: Starting from Fermi's golden rule, the transfer rate is expressed as an overlap between the exciton near-field spectrum and graphene's long-wavelength electronic loss function, weighted by an exciton form factor. A Gaussian form factor models moiré exciton spatial extent. A Pauli-blocking model treats graphene as a gate-tunable bath. The model is benchmarked against full RPA loss function.
AI.result: The model reproduces the established $z^{-4}$ law in the point-dipole limit. For $z\lesssim\lX$, high-momentum near-field components are filtered out, making the transfer rate sensitive to exciton localization. Pauli blocking suppresses interband excitations when $2|\muF|\approx\hbar\omega$, partially restoring PL intensity. The minimal model matches full RPA within a few percent. PL observables are mapped over relevant parameter ranges.
AI.conclusion: Graphene acts as a tunable 2D electronic reservoir whose long-wavelength response can be probed via exciton PL quenching, rather than just a passive electrostatic element in TMD/hBN/graphene heterostructures.

title: Modulation theory formulation of atomic light-matter interaction
summary: We provide a re-formulation of the light-matter interaction of trapped-atom systems in terms of classical modulation theory. We introduce commuting ``mean'' quadrature operators together with ``deviation'' operators that describe the quantum fluctuations resulting from the uncertainty principle. From the ``mean'' position operator stems an accurate approximate expression for the internal transition coupling strengths in terms of Bessel functions which matches that of classical modulation theory. The error of the approximation is a direct result of quantum fluctuations. We also show that this result can also be obtained with WKB theory. The validity of our approach is numerically verified and supported by an expansion of the exact expression using a recurrence relation between orthogonal polynomials. Compared to the exact solution, our result is analytically more tractable, numerically more stable, and admits a transparent physical interpretation which connects the classical and quantum pictures.

AI.tldr: The paper reformulates light-matter interaction in trapped-atom systems using classical modulation theory, introducing mean and deviation quadrature operators to derive Bessel function-based approximations for transition coupling strengths, with connections to WKB theory and numerical verification.
AI.motivation: To bridge the classical and quantum descriptions of light-matter interaction in trapped-atom systems by re-formulating the problem in terms of classical modulation theory, while accounting for quantum fluctuations via deviation operators.
AI.method: Introduces commuting mean quadrature operators and deviation operators to describe quantum fluctuations; derives approximate expressions for internal transition coupling strengths using Bessel functions; employs WKB theory as an alternative derivation; validates via numerical expansion using recurrence relations between orthogonal polynomials.
AI.result: The derived Bessel function approximation matches classical modulation theory, with errors attributable to quantum fluctuations. The approach is numerically stable and analytically tractable.
AI.conclusion: The reformulation provides a transparent physical interpretation connecting classical and quantum pictures, with advantages in analytical tractability and numerical stability over the exact solution.

title: High-order tensor neural network for iteration-free structure relaxation
summary: Structure relaxation is important for the discovery of new materials, yet conventional ab initio optimization remains a major bottleneck in high-throughput screening workflows. Machine learning potentials have accelerated relaxation by orders of magnitude, but they still rely on iterative optimization and high-quality DFT force labels. Here, we present HotRelax, a high-order tensor message-passing neural network for one-shot, end-to-end prediction of relaxed structures. Trained directly on paired unrelaxed and relaxed structures, HotRelax requires no DFT force labels and predicts relaxed structures in a single forward pass, without iterative inference or post-processing. Across five diverse datasets spanning 3D bulk crystals, 2D layered materials and catalysts, HotRelax shows strong performance relative to state-of-the-art end-to-end relaxation models, achieving lower prediction errors on several benchmarks while maintaining a compact model size and efficient inference. Extensive DFT calculations further show that the predicted structures are close in energy to their DFT-relaxed counterparts. When integrated into catalytic workflows, HotRelax also improves the accuracy and generalization of relaxed-state energy prediction models. Together, these results support HotRelax as an efficient and widely applicable framework for end-to-end structure relaxation, with strong potential to accelerate high-throughput materials discovery.

AI.tldr: HotRelax is a high-order tensor message-passing neural network that predicts relaxed material structures in a single forward pass without DFT force labels or iterative optimization, achieving strong performance across bulk crystals, 2D materials, and catalysts.
AI.motivation: Ab initio structure relaxation is a major bottleneck in high-throughput materials discovery due to its computational cost, and existing machine learning potentials still require iterative optimization and expensive DFT force labels.
AI.method: HotRelax employs a high-order tensor message-passing neural network trained directly on paired unrelaxed and relaxed structures to predict relaxed structures in a single forward pass, without iterative inference, post-processing, or DFT force labels.
AI.result: Across 3D bulk crystals, 2D layered materials, and catalysts, HotRelax achieves lower prediction errors than state-of-the-art end-to-end relaxation models with compact model size and efficient inference; predicted structures are close in energy to DFT-relaxed counterparts.
AI.conclusion: HotRelax provides an efficient and widely applicable framework for end-to-end structure relaxation, with strong potential to accelerate high-throughput materials discovery.

title: Phase Time Crystals and Pairing in Binary Active Chiral Systems
summary: We introduce a class of dynamic systems we call phase time crystals consisting of a binary assembly of particles with intermediate or long-range repulsive interactions that are subjected to a circular drive of uniform chirality in which each particle species is out of phase from the other by 180 degrees. As a function of the particle density and orbit radius, this system can organize into a rich variety of dynamical crystalline states, including one in which the out of phase particles form bound pairs that assemble into a triangular lattice. We also find stripe phases, overlapping packed crystals, disordered or phase glass states with no diffusion, mixed fluids, and different types of phase-separated states. We show that these states are robust against the addition of thermal fluctuations, and that the paired crystal can melt into a paired fluid. If the drive on each particle species is of opposite chirality, the system forms stripes and packed lattices, but no paired crystal is present. We demonstrate that by modifying the nature of the chiral driving, it is possible to realize numerous kinds of active molecular lattices, including dynamic square spin ice geometries and higher-order complex structures.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces "phase time crystals," a binary particle system with repulsive interactions under circular chiral driving where species are 180° out of phase, yielding diverse dynamical crystalline states, paired triangular lattices, stripe phases, glass states, and active molecular lattices like square spin ice.
AI.motivation: To explore a new class of non-equilibrium dynamical systems (phase time crystals) that can self-organize into rich crystalline and complex structures under chiral driving with out-of-phase species, and to understand their stability and phase behavior.
AI.method: The authors simulate a binary assembly of particles with intermediate/long-range repulsive interactions subjected to a circular drive of uniform chirality, with each species 180° out of phase. They vary particle density and orbit radius, and examine opposite chirality cases and thermal fluctuations.
AI.result: The system exhibits a rich variety of states: bound pairs forming triangular lattices, stripe phases, overlapping packed crystals, phase glass states (disordered with no diffusion), mixed fluids, and phase-separated states. These are robust against thermal fluctuations. Opposite chirality yields stripes and packed lattices but no paired crystal. Modified chiral driving produces active molecular lattices including dynamic square spin ice and higher-order complex structures.
AI.conclusion: Phase time crystals represent a versatile platform for realizing diverse dynamical ordered phases and active molecular crystals, with potential for designing complex non-equilibrium structures.

title: Theory of High-Tc Superconductivity in Cuprates
summary:
The essential physical processes underlying the phenomenon of High-Tc superconductivity in cuprates occur in the $CuO_2$ planes, found in these materials. The dynamics of the active electrons belonging to such planes is well described by the Three Bands Hubbard Model (3BHM). The complexity of such model, however, led the researchers to look for simpler and yet relevant alternatives. In the attempts to circumvent the complexity of this model,two main simplified versions of the (3BHM) were considered. In the first alternative, one eliminates the doped holes and their respective sub-lattices by tying them to the $Cu^{++}$ electrons, thereby forming the so called Zhang-Rice singlets. The remaining dynamics consists in doping a Mott-Hubbard insulator and is described by the t-J Model. The second alternative
  maintains that the $Cu^{++}$ electrons form a square lattice of localized spins, while the doped holes move along the oxygen sub-lattices and undergo a Kondo like magnetic interaction with the localized spins, besides the Hubbard-like electric repulsion. This scenario is described by the Spin-Fermion-Hubbard Model. Most of the researchers in the field chose to follow the first road, while, I chose the second one. In this article I review in detail the reasons why that choice has led to a successful theory for High-Tc superconductivity in hole doped cuprates.

AI.tldr: The author reviews why choosing the Spin-Fermion-Hubbard Model over the t-J Model (Zhang-Rice singlets) as a simplification of the Three Bands Hubbard Model leads to a successful theory for High-Tc superconductivity in hole-doped cuprates.
AI.motivation: To explain why the Spin-Fermion-Hubbard Model, rather than the more popular t-J Model, provides a more successful theoretical framework for understanding High-Tc superconductivity in hole-doped cuprates.
AI.method: The author compares two simplified versions of the Three Bands Hubbard Model: (1) the t-J Model, based on Zhang-Rice singlet formation, and (2) the Spin-Fermion-Hubbard Model, where Cu++ electrons form a localized spin lattice and doped holes move on oxygen sub-lattices with Kondo-like interaction. The author advocates for and reviews the second approach.
AI.result: The Spin-Fermion-Hubbard Model (the author's chosen path) yields a successful theory for High-Tc superconductivity in hole-doped cuprates, in contrast to the t-J Model favored by most researchers.
AI.conclusion: The choice of the Spin-Fermion-Hubbard Model over the t-J Model is justified by its success in explaining High-Tc superconductivity in hole-doped cuprates.

title: Atomically Thin Amorphous Carbon with an Ultralow Dielectric Constant
summary: Two-dimensional (2D) materials exhibit excellent properties at monolayer thickness and are viable replacements for various microelectronic components as scaling gradually approaches the atomic limit. Despite significant advancements in the ongoing 2D revolution of integrated circuits, one crucial building block, namely a 2D ultralow-k (ULK) dielectric, remains unreported. The challenge lies in achieving a dielectric constant less than 3, as traditional low-k dielectrics are inherently unstable at the 2D limit due to their amorphous or porous nature. The realisation of ultrathin dielectrics with low-k is also needed to address current bottlenecks in integrated circuits scaling. Specifically, low-k materials are necessary to minimise parasitic capacitances as the distance between conductive elements shrinks below 10 nm. Moreover, advanced architectures like gate-all-around field effect transistors (GAA FET) require even lower dielectric constants (k<2) at sub-3nm thickness. Here, we show that layer-by-layer grown multilayer amorphous carbon (ML-AC), as thin as 0.8 nm, is a mechanically robust 2D ULK dielectric with k of 1.35 and dielectric strength of 28-31 MV cm-1. The lack of any long-range order, its intrinsic 2D nature, sp2 carbon character and low density are all essential for minimising dielectric permittivity. Moreover, ML-AC overcomes the vulnerability of existing dielectrics to ion diffusion degradation with a record metal ion diffusion time to failure (TTF) of 10^10 s for even a single layer. Therefore, otherwise necessary additional layers occupying up to 3 nm can be eliminated, which is especially significant as metal line widths approach 10 nm. Combined with its low-temperature, direct and conformal growth even on a dielectric, these critical features enable substantial improvements in silicon-based semiconductor electronics and ensure compatibility with future 2D electronics.

AI.tldr: The paper reports the first demonstration of a two-dimensional ultralow-k dielectric material—multilayer amorphous carbon (ML-AC) as thin as 0.8 nm—with a dielectric constant of 1.35, high dielectric strength (28-31 MV cm⁻¹), and exceptional resistance to metal ion diffusion, addressing a critical missing component in the 2D revolution of integrated circuits.
AI.motivation: A 2D ultralow-k (k<3) dielectric has remained unreported despite progress in 2D integrated circuits, and traditional low-k dielectrics are unstable at the 2D limit due to amorphous/porous nature. Ultrathin low-k materials are needed to minimize parasitic capacitances as interconnect distances shrink below 10 nm and for advanced architectures like GAA FETs requiring k<2 at sub-3 nm thickness.
AI.method: Layer-by-layer grown multilayer amorphous carbon (ML-AC) films as thin as 0.8 nm were synthesized and characterized for dielectric constant, dielectric strength, mechanical robustness, and resistance to metal ion diffusion.
AI.result: ML-AC achieves k=1.35, dielectric strength of 28-31 MV cm⁻¹, and a record metal ion diffusion time to failure of 10¹⁰ s for a single layer, eliminating the need for additional barrier layers up to 3 nm thick.
AI.conclusion: ML-AC is a mechanically robust 2D ULK dielectric that overcomes key scaling bottlenecks in silicon-based and future 2D electronics, enabled by its lack of long-range order, 2D nature, sp² carbon character, and low density, along with low-temperature direct and conformal growth compatibility.

title: Sixteen-Fold Way for Fermionic Topological Orders
summary: Fermionic topological orders can host 't Hooft anomalies with no bosonic counterpart. We identify a new sixteen-fold family of (2+1)D fermionic topological orders, forming a fermionic analogue of Kitaev's sixteen-fold way. This family is distinguished by the mod 16 't Hooft anomaly of a $\mathbb{Z}_2$ one-form symmetry, generated in each theory by a single nontrivial $\mathbb{Z}_2$ anyon. This intrinsically fermionic anomaly permits anyon spins that are forbidden in bosonic phases; the simplest new example is an Abelian fermionic topological order containing a single $\mathbb{Z}_2$ Abelian anyon of spin 1/8. Each theory can be realized as the gapped boundary of a (3+1)D fermionic symmetry-protected topological (SPT) phase protected by the $\mathbb{Z}_2$ one-form symmetry, which acquires a $\mathbb{Z}_{16}$ classification once the spacetime spin structure is twisted by the one-form symmetry. We realize these phases microscopically via lattice models built from Walker-Wang models coupled to local fermions.

AI.tldr: This paper identifies a new sixteen-fold family of (2+1)D fermionic topological orders with intrinsically fermionic 't Hooft anomalies of a ℤ₂ one-form symmetry, forming a fermionic analogue of Kitaev's sixteen-fold way, and realizes them as gapped boundaries of (3+1)D fermionic SPT phases with ℤ₁₆ classification.
AI.motivation: To discover and characterize fermionic topological orders that host 't Hooft anomalies with no bosonic counterpart, extending the understanding of topological phases beyond bosonic systems.
AI.method: The authors use field-theoretic anomaly analysis, classification of anyon spins modulo 1/16 constructions, and microscopic lattice models based on Walker-Wang models coupled to local fermions.
AI.result: A sixteen-fold family of (2+1)D fermionic topological orders distinguished by a mod 16 't Hooft anomaly of a ℤ₂ one-form symmetry, with the simplest new example being an Abelian topological order containing a single ℤ₂ anyon of spin 1/8.
AI.conclusion: These intrinsically fermionic topological orders can be realized as gapped boundaries of (3+1)D fermionic SPT phases with ℤ₁₆ classification, where the spacetime spin structure is twisted by the one-form symmetry.

title: Structural relaxation and stagnation of grain boundary during migration
summary: Instability is a major bottleneck in nanomaterials due to grain boundary (GB) activities under thermal or mechanical stimuli. The relaxation of GB will stabilize the properties of materials by structure modification of GBs to lower energy states. However, lack of understanding of mechanisms limits the application of GB relaxation. In this study, we certify that GB can realize relaxation through defect emission including vacancy, twinning and dislocations, etc, which lower the average atomic energy of GB. In particular, we found stagnation and shear-coupling migration accompany the relaxation process, where a lower average atomic energy and lower average atomic volume of grain boundaries can be the reasons for stagnation. In this study, we found when simulated by ramped energy-conserving orientated driving force, under a specific driving force, the grain boundary suddenly stops migrating during the migration process, and as the driving force increases to a certain value, the grain boundary continues to migrate. Even at fixed driving forces, the grain boundary migration process can stall. This phenomenon has been found in many grain boundaries, and it has been found that the reason for the stagnation is the change of the average atomic energy of grain boundaries and the average atomic volume of grain boundaries. The discovery of this stagnation phenomenon is helpful to better understand the migration characteristics of grain boundaries and lays a foundation for improving the strength of materials by designing grain boundary microstructures.

AI.tldr: This study demonstrates that grain boundary relaxation in nanomaterials occurs through defect emission (vacancies, twinning, dislocations), lowering average atomic energy. A stagnation phenomenon in GB migration is discovered under both ramped and fixed driving forces, attributed to changes in average atomic energy and volume of GBs, providing insights for designing stronger materials.
AI.motivation: Instability caused by grain boundary activities is a major bottleneck in nanomaterials. While GB relaxation can stabilize materials by lowering energy states, the mechanisms behind GB relaxation are poorly understood, limiting its application.
AI.method: Simulations using ramped energy-conserving orientated driving force to study GB relaxation, defect emission, migration, and stagnation phenomena across multiple grain boundaries.
AI.result: GB relaxation occurs via defect emission (vacancies, twinning, dislocations) lowering average atomic energy. Stagnation and shear-coupling migration accompany relaxation. Under specific driving forces, GB migration can suddenly stop and restart when force increases. Stagnation correlates with reduced average atomic energy and volume of GBs.
AI.conclusion: The discovery of stagnation phenomena in GB migration improves understanding of GB migration characteristics and lays a foundation for enhancing material strength through design of GB microstructures.

title: Direct observation of interfacial exchange coupling in a magnetic tunnel junction through spin-polarized quasiparticle interference
summary: Interfacial exchange coupling plays a critical role in enabling novel phenomena in magnetic heterostructures, such as spin triplet superconductivity, quantum anomalous Hall effect (QAHE), and advanced spintronic functionalities. While microscopic characterization of this coupling is essential for elucidating the underlying mechanism, it remains technically challenging. Here, using spin-polarized scanning tunneling microscopy (SP-STM) and quasiparticle interference, we directly observed interfacial exchange coupling in a magnetic tunnel junction formed by an Fe coated tip and a Cr(001) surface. We found the ferromagnetic tip induces significant energy shift (up to 10 meV) in the spin-polarized surface state of Cr(001). This shift is highly sensitive to the tip-surface distance and the spin-alignment between Fe tip and Cr surface, which can be switched by external magnetic field. Our results demonstrate that extended 2D surface states can mediate strong exchange coupling across a heterojunction, enabling local control of interfacial exchange interaction induced phenomena.

AI.tldr: Using spin-polarized STM, researchers directly observed interfacial exchange coupling in an Fe tip/Cr(001) magnetic tunnel junction, finding a significant energy shift (up to 10 meV) in Cr's spin-polarized surface state that is sensitive to tip-surface distance and spin alignment, demonstrating that extended 2D surface states can mediate strong exchange coupling across heterojunctions.
AI.motivation: Interfacial exchange coupling is critical for novel magnetic heterostructure phenomena (e.g., spin triplet superconductivity, QAHE), but its microscopic characterization has remained technically challenging.
AI.method: Spin-polarized scanning tunneling microscopy (SP-STM) combined with quasiparticle interference analysis to observe interfacial exchange coupling in an Fe-coated tip/Cr(001) magnetic tunnel junction.
AI.result: The ferromagnetic tip induces up to 10 meV energy shift in the spin-polarized surface state of Cr(001); this shift depends on tip-surface distance and spin alignment (switchable by external magnetic field).
AI.conclusion: Extended 2D surface states can mediate strong exchange coupling across a heterojunction, enabling local control of interfacial exchange interaction induced phenomena.

title: Non-linear control variate in δf particle-in-cell methods using symplectic neural networks
summary: We present a novel δf particle-in-cell (PIC) method for the kinetic simulation of electrostatic plasmas in which the bulk density, acting as a control variate, is evolved using symplectic neural networks (SympNets). The SympNets are used as an approximation of the backward flow and trained using the particle trajectories. We introduce a periodic variant of the SympNet architecture that encodes the spatial periodicity of the problem into the network itself. We validate the approach with numerical results in 1D1V and 3D3V for the Vlasov-Poisson system.

AI.tldr: A novel δf PIC method for electrostatic plasmas uses SympNets to evolve the bulk density as a control variate, with a periodic SympNet architecture, validated on Vlasov-Poisson systems in 1D1V and 3D3V.
AI.motivation: To improve the δf PIC method for kinetic plasma simulation by using symplectic neural networks to evolve the bulk density (control variate), reducing variance and improving accuracy in electrostatic plasma simulations.
AI.method: The authors introduce a δf PIC method where the bulk density is evolved via SympNets that approximate the backward flow. A novel periodic SympNet architecture is designed to encode spatial periodicity. The networks are trained on particle trajectories.
AI.result: The method is validated with numerical experiments in 1D1V and 3D3V for the Vlasov-Poisson system, demonstrating its effectiveness.
AI.conclusion: The proposed hybrid approach combining δf PIC with SympNets offers a promising variance reduction technique for kinetic plasma simulations, with the periodic architecture being a key enabler for problems with spatial periodicity.

title: Forward-backward correspondence between stationary structure and splitting probabilities in active matter
summary: Active particles confined by hard walls accumulate at boundaries and may become dynamically adsorbed due to directional persistence. In this work, we show that the same persistence mechanism also gives rise to a finite wall splitting probability, meaning that a particle initialized at a wall can reach the opposite boundary before returning to its starting point. By comparing forward and backward evolution equations directly in position--velocity phase space, we derive exact relations linking stationary distributions and splitting probabilities for run-and-tumble, active Brownian, and active Ornstein--Uhlenbeck particles. In particular, we show that the stationary density is generated by the spatial derivative of the splitting probability, while the distribution of dynamically adsorbed particles at the walls is encoded in wall splitting probabilities. The correspondence is valid in arbitrary spatial dimension and establishes an exact bridge between stationary and first-passage descriptions of confined active matter, revealing them as complementary representations of the same persistence-driven dynamics.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that directional persistence in active particles leads to a finite wall splitting probability (particles going from one wall to opposite boundary before returning), and derives exact relations linking stationary distributions and splitting probabilities for three active particle models, establishing a bridge between stationary and first-passage descriptions.
AI.motivation: Active particles confined by hard walls accumulate at boundaries due to directional persistence; the authors aim to understand the probabilistic structure of this phenomenon and connect stationary properties with first-passage characteristics.
AI.method: The authors compare forward and backward evolution equations in position-velocity phase space for run-and-tumble, active Brownian, and active Ornstein-Uhlenbeck particles, deriving exact relations between stationary distributions and splitting probabilities.
AI.result: The stationary density is generated by the spatial derivative of the splitting probability, and the distribution of dynamically adsorbed particles at walls is encoded in wall splitting probabilities. The correspondence holds in arbitrary spatial dimension.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes an exact bridge between stationary and first-passage descriptions of confined active matter, revealing them as complementary representations of persistence-driven dynamics.

title: 40 years of cuprate high-Tc superconductors: a perspective on theories
summary: An attempt is made to give a brief but coherent account of the situation of the theoretical ideas in addressing the mechanism of superconductivity in cuprate high-Tc superconductors. Specifically, the idea of superconductivity from repulsive interactions is discussed as it is gaining ground since the `consensus' paper was written in 2015\cite{kei}. The challenges it faces is also discussed. Three main schools of thought are presented, and an experimental result of 2022 pertaining to Anderson's super-exchange mechanism is also discussed. An updated list of Anderson's ``dogmas" is also presented, as after year 2000, many other universally applicable experimental facts has been discovered. The ``dogmas" are universal facts which are distilled from a variety of complex experimental results, and highlights the key findings that seems to be central to the mechanism of superconductivity in cuprates. These are discussed as a commemoration of 40 years of high-Tc cuprate research.

AI.tldr: This paper reviews theoretical progress on the mechanism of superconductivity in cuprate high-Tc superconductors, focusing on repulsive-interaction-based superconductivity since 2015, three main schools of thought, experimental evidence (2022) for Anderson's super-exchange mechanism, and an updated set of Anderson's "dogmas" (universal experimental facts) to mark 40 years of cuprate research.
AI.motivation: To provide a coherent account of theoretical ideas addressing the mechanism of superconductivity in cuprate high-Tc superconductors, particularly the repulsive interaction framework, as a commemoration of 40 years of research in this field.
AI.method: The paper reviews theoretical schools of thought, discusses the 2022 experimental result on Anderson's super-exchange mechanism, and distills universal experimental facts (Anderson's "dogmas") from complex experimental data.
AI.result: Three main schools of thought are identified; the 2022 experimental result pertaining to Anderson's super-exchange mechanism is discussed; an updated list of Anderson's "dogmas" (universal facts central to cuprate superconductivity) is presented, incorporating discoveries made after 2000.
AI.conclusion: The repulsive-interaction-based superconductivity idea has gained ground since 2015, but challenges remain; the updated dogmas highlight key findings central to understanding cuprate superconductivity, commemorating 40 years of research.

title: Microfabricated Au and Au/graphene bilayer platelets for levitation experiments
summary: We describe a fabrication process for preparing liquid suspensions of micron-scale Au and Au/graphene bilayer platelets using thin-film deposition, optical lithography, ion milling, hydrofluoric acid (HF) substrate etching, and release from the substrate into a liquid suspension. Residual HF is removed through repeated centrifugation, decanting, and dilution cycles. The resulting suspension is characterized by electrospray deposition onto a secondary substrate, followed by electron and atomic force microscopy. The deposited platelets exhibit minimal aggregation, and the overall platelet yield reaches up to 30% of the platelets originally patterned on the wafer. Lateral force microscopy further confirms that the Au/graphene bilayer remains intact throughout fabrication, release, and electrospray deposition. This process provides a practical route for preparing high-quality platelet suspensions for levitated nanoparticle experiments and other applications requiring suspensions of two-dimensional nanostructures.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a fabrication process for producing liquid suspensions of micron-scale Au and Au/graphene bilayer platelets, achieving up to 30% yield with minimal aggregation and structural integrity confirmed by microscopy.
AI.motivation: To develop a practical and reliable method for preparing high-quality suspensions of micron-scale metallic and bilayer nanostructures for use in levitated nanoparticle experiments and other applications requiring suspended two-dimensional materials.
AI.method: The process combines thin-film deposition, optical lithography, ion milling, and HF substrate etching to produce platelets, followed by repeated centrifugation/decanting/dilution cycles to remove residual HF. The suspension is characterized via electrospray deposition, electron microscopy, atomic force microscopy, and lateral force microscopy.
AI.result: Deposited platelets show minimal aggregation, a platelet yield of up to 30%, and Au/graphene bilayer integrity is preserved throughout the entire process chain.
AI.conclusion: This fabrication route offers a practical, scalable method for producing high-quality platelet suspensions suitable for levitated nanoparticle studies and other applications involving two-dimensional nanostructures in suspension.

title: Survival of the metallic state in a single-hole multiband $p$-orbital molecular system
summary: Strong correlations and ferromagnetic Hund's coupling lead to diverse electronic phenomena in transition-metal oxides that sensitively depend on the $d$-orbital electron filling. Fullerides, their $p$-electron counterparts, exhibit effective antiferromagnetic Hund's coupling in a different energy range. At half-filling ($n=3$, three electrons in triply degenerate orbitals), both $d-$ and $p$-electron systems are Mott insulators due to strong correlations and Hund's coupling. Away from half-filling, in single-electron/hole ($n=1,5$) $d$-orbital systems, Hund's coupling opposes the correlations, reducing the Mott gap and allowing survival of metallicity. Here we report a single-hole multiorbital correlated $p$-electron system, orthorhombic-structured Yb$_2$CsC$_{60}$ comprising pentavalent C$_{60}^{5-}$ anions, which also exhibits a robust metallic state with no Mott transition, just like in the metastable single-electron cubic-structured CsC$_{60}$. We assert that particle-hole symmetry holds well in ($n=1,5$) fullerides and that their $p$-electron-derived states are analogous to those in $d$-orbital solids, providing impetus for further study of these correlated systems.

AI.motivation: To investigate whether p-electron fulleride systems exhibit similar correlation physics to d-electron transition-metal oxides, particularly the survival of metallicity away from half-filling due to Hund's coupling, and to test particle-hole symmetry in single-hole/single-electron fullerides.
AI.method: The study examines orthorhombic-structured Yb₂CsC₆₀ containing pentavalent C₆₀⁵⁻ anions (single-hole, n=5 in triply degenerate orbitals) and compares its electronic properties to the metastable single-electron cubic CsC₆₀ (n=1).
AI.result: The single-hole p-electron system Yb₂CsC₆₀ exhibits a robust metallic state with no Mott transition, analogous to the single-electron d-orbital system CsC₆₀. Particle-hole symmetry holds well for (n=1,5) fullerides.
AI.conclusion: In single-hole/single-electron fullerides (n=1,5), Hund's coupling opposes correlations and prevents Mott transition, preserving metallicity. These p-electron systems behave analogously to d-orbital transition-metal oxides, warranting further study.

title: Strain engineering of ultrafast magnetism in the room-temperature vdW ferromagnet Fe3GaTe2
summary: Controlling ultrafast magnetic dynamics is critical to understanding nonequilibrium spin interactions and advancing high-speed spintronics. However, a lack of efficient in situ tuning strategies leaves most ultrafast studies largely dependent on the intrinsic properties of the individual materials. Here we demonstrate continuous strain tuning of both the equilibrium magnetic response and ultrafast demagnetization dynamics in the room-temperature van der Waals ferromagnet Fe3GaTe2. Applying up to 4.2% uniaxial tensile strain increases the coercive field from nearly zero to 100 Oe, consistent with an enhancement of the effective perpendicular magnetic anisotropy. Time-resolved magneto-optical Kerr effect measurements further reveal strain-accelerated ultrafast demagnetization, with 1.2% tensile strain reducing the characteristic demagnetization time by approximately 20%. Remarkably, strain accesses an accelerated demagnetization regime that cannot be reached simply by increasing pump fluence in the unstrained sample. Combined with first-principles calculations, our results resolve that the applied strain modifies the spin-lattice energy transfer, leading to the observed accelerated demagnetization. These findings establish mechanical strain as an effective route for on-demand control of ultrafast magnetic dynamics while reducing the required optical energy by reconfiguring the magnetic energy landscape and associated spin-relaxation pathways.

AI.method: The authors apply uniaxial tensile strain (up to 4.2%) to Fe3GaTe2, measure equilibrium magnetic response via coercive field changes, probe ultrafast demagnetization using time-resolved magneto-optical Kerr effect (TR-MOKE), and perform first-principles calculations to interpret the mechanism.

title: Multi-level π-junction in a proximitized Ge/SiGe quantum dot probed by an on-chip superconducting microwave resonator
summary: Using on-chip microwave measurements, we investigate multilevel $π$-junctions formed by proximitized quantum dot (QD) in a germanium (Ge)/silicon-germanium (SiGe) heterostructure. In the multilevel regime, where several QD orbitals contribute simultaneously to superconducting transport, the Josephson ground state is no longer determined solely by the occupation of a single orbital. By combining DC transport and microwave techniques, we identify the qualitative signatures of multilevel $π$-junctions in both their gate-voltage dependence and microwave response. In particular, we observe combinations phase transitions that are sharp or smooth in gate voltage and which exhibit distinct inductive and dissipative signatures. Such multilevel Josephson transport has previously been observed primarily in exceptionally clean systems such as carbon nanotubes. Our results establish proximitized Ge as a platform for investigating hybrid superconductor/semiconductor physics and demonstrate the integration of gate-defined superconducting quantum devices with high-quality on-chip microwave resonators.

It establishes Ge as a platform for hybrid superconductor/semiconductor physics.
