We identify that the pure double stripe spin state is unstable in La$_3$Ni$_2$O$_7$ towards a commensurate charge-density wave instability, which favors a spin-modulated double stripe order with intertwined charge and spin instabilities and establish the hierarchy of ordered states in La$_3$Ni$_2$O$_7$, providing an important link between its ambient-pressure and superconducting high-pressure phases. We further discuss our results in the context of available experimental literature and propose further experimental tests to elucidate the origin of the SDW/DW states in this system.

AI.tldr: Using unrestricted Hartree-Fock calculations, the authors identify the second density-wave transition at ~130 K in La$_3$Ni$_2$O$_7$ as originating from a charge-density wave instability intertwined with a double-stripe spin-density wave, establishing a hierarchy of ordered states linking ambient-pressure and high-pressure superconducting phases.
AI.motivation: To resolve the unresolved origin of the second density-wave transition (T_DW ≈ 130 K) in La$_3$Ni$_2$O$_7$, which is crucial for understanding the material's pressure-induced high-temperature superconductivity.
AI.method: Unrestricted Hartree-Fock calculations, analyzing instabilities within the orthorhombic phase with lifted degeneracy between ordering wavevectors Q_Y=(0,π) and Q_X=(π,0).
AI.result: The pure double-stripe spin state (with ordering vector Q_Y=(0,π)) is unstable towards a commensurate charge-density wave instability, leading to a spin-modulated double-stripe order with intertwined charge and spin instabilities.
AI.conclusion: Establishes the hierarchy of ordered states in La$_3$Ni$_2$O$_7$, linking ambient-pressure density-wave states to the high-pressure superconducting phase, and proposes experimental tests to further elucidate the SDW/DW states.

title: Kinetically Controlled Condensation Boundary Governing Indium Incorporation in InGaN Metal Organic Vapor Phase Epitaxy
summary: We combine in situ synchrotron X-ray crystal truncation rod measurements with a binary Burton-Cabrera-Frank model to quantify indium incorporation during InGaN growth by metal-organic vapor phase epitaxy (MOVPE) on GaN(0001). By distinguishing In adatoms from condensed droplets and incorporating coupled Ga-In incorporation kinetics, the model captures the intrinsically nonlinear dependence of indium composition on precursor flux and growth temperature. The critical In coverage corresponding to the maximum attainable In composition at a given temperature is determined by a kinetic balance between In adatom supply and incorporation capacity, defining a kinetically controlled condensation boundary that shifts with temperature and Ga flux. The model quantitatively predicts this boundary, in agreement with independent measurements, and provides a predictive framework for optimizing high-In-content InGaN growth while avoiding droplet formation.

AI.tldr: A combined experimental and modeling study quantifies indium incorporation during InGaN MOVPE growth, capturing nonlinear composition dependence on precursor flux and temperature via a binary Burton-Cabrera-Frank model that distinguishes adatoms from droplets, and defines a kinetically controlled condensation boundary for optimizing high-In-content growth.
AI.motivation: To understand and quantify the intrinsically nonlinear indium incorporation behavior during InGaN MOVPE growth, particularly the competition between In adatom incorporation and droplet formation, which limits achievable In composition.
AI.method: In situ synchrotron X-ray crystal truncation rod measurements combined with a binary Burton-Cabrera-Frank model that distinguishes In adatoms from condensed droplets and incorporates coupled Ga-In incorporation kinetics.
AI.result: The model captures the nonlinear dependence of indium composition on precursor flux and growth temperature; identifies a critical In coverage defining a kinetically controlled condensation boundary that shifts with temperature and Ga flux; quantitatively predicts this boundary in agreement with independent measurements.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides a predictive tool for optimizing high-In-content InGaN growth while avoiding droplet formation.

title: Synchronic scattering and geometric dephasing in microwave-induced resistance oscillations
summary:
We present a novel quantum transport model for microwave-induced resistance oscillations (MIRO) where we prove that the instantaneous scattering rate is directly modulated by the velocity of the driven coherent state. This interaction peaks exactly at $ωt = 2nπ$, where the wave packets sweep through the impurity landscape at maximum speed, breaking time-reversal symmetry to generate a net direct current. Additionally, we introduce a dephasing architecture to explain amplitude saturation: a non-linear geometric dephasing ($\exp(-A/R_c)$) triggered when the displacement amplitude $A$ of the oscillating coherent state,
  approaches the cyclotron radius $R_{c}$. This perfectly captures the linear-to-sublinear power crossover at high intensities, offering a fully coherent description of non-equilibrium transport.

AI.tldr: A quantum transport model shows microwave-induced resistance oscillations arise from velocity-modulated scattering of a driven coherent state, with amplitude saturation explained by nonlinear geometric dephasing when displacement approaches the cyclotron radius.
AI.motivation: To provide a fully coherent quantum description of microwave-induced resistance oscillations (MIRO) and explain the amplitude saturation and power crossover observed in experiments.
AI.method: The authors develop a quantum transport model where the instantaneous scattering rate is modulated by the velocity of a driven coherent state, peaking at ωt = 2nπ. A dephasing architecture with nonlinear geometric dephasing exp(-A/R_c) is introduced when displacement amplitude A approaches cyclotron radius R_c.
AI.result: The model captures the linear-to-sublinear power crossover at high intensities and demonstrates that time-reversal symmetry breaking at maximum wave packet sweep speed generates a net direct current.
AI.conclusion: The framework offers a fully coherent description of non-equilibrium transport in MIRO, successfully explaining both the oscillation mechanism and amplitude saturation effects.

title: Trimers in the Extended Hubbard Model
summary: The Lieb theorem is a cornerstone of quantum magnetism theory in condensed matter. In this work, we investigate the instability of the Lieb insulating ferrimagnetic phase in the extended Hubbard model on a trimer chain at half-filling, with one electron per site, under increasing the nearest-neighbor Coulomb coupling $V$. Our results show that despite a noticeable increase in doublon density with $V$, the ferrimagnetic insulating phase remains robust up to the phase separation (PS) line, which is observed at $V \gtrsim U/4$, where $U$ is the local Coulomb repulsion. Above the PS line, one of the coexisting phases is primarily populated by doublons on one of the two sublattices of the chain. This phase coexists with a metallic, unsaturated ferromagnetic phase for $U \gtrsim t$, and with a singlet phase for $U \lesssim t$, where $t$ is the intra-trimer hopping amplitude. We estimate the PS and the crossover lines with the help of density matrix renormalization group calculations.

AI.tldr: The Lieb insulating ferrimagnetic phase in the extended Hubbard model on a trimer chain at half-filling remains robust up to a phase separation line at V ≳ U/4, above which different coexisting phases emerge depending on the relative strength of U and t.
AI.motivation: To investigate the instability of the Lieb insulating ferrimagnetic phase under increasing nearest-neighbor Coulomb coupling V in the extended Hubbard model on a trimer chain at half-filling.
AI.method: Density matrix renormalization group (DMRG) calculations to estimate phase separation and crossover lines.
AI.result: The ferrimagnetic insulating phase is robust up to V ≳ U/4. Above PS line: for U ≳ t, a doublon-rich phase coexists with a metallic unsaturated ferromagnetic phase; for U ≲ t, it coexists with a singlet phase.
AI.conclusion: The Lieb ferrimagnetic phase shows remarkable stability against nearest-neighbor repulsion, only destabilizing via phase separation beyond a threshold coupling strength.

title: Silicon-compatible ideal antiferroelectricity with large digital electromechanical responses enabled by thermal-strain domain engineering
summary: Antiferroelectrics exhibit reversible antipolar-polar transformations, offering a compelling platform for multiple functionalities in modern nanoelectronics, yet deterministic control of antiferroelectric domains and switching pathways remain elusive. Moreover, their integration with ubiquitous silicon-based electronic devices has been limited by the structural and chemical incompatibilities of conventional oxide platforms. Here, we convert the conventional drawback of thermal mismatch into a functional advantage and realize ideal antiferroelectricity in epitaxial PbZrO3 thin films on silicon through thermal tensile-strain engineering, a strain regime unattainable on conventional perovskite substrates. Combined theoretical and experimental studies show that tensile strain stabilizes the (004)o domain, enabling a direct one-step switching, whereas compressive-strain-stabilized (240)o domains switch through intermediate ferrielectric states. The resulting films exhibit near-zero remanent polarization, square double hysteresis, nanosecond switching (~75ns), large reversible electrostrain (~0.6%) and robust operation windows. These findings provide key insights into domain-engineered ideal antiferroelectricity on silicon, opening a viable route toward high-performance antiferroelectric nano-electronic devices.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates ideal antiferroelectricity in epitaxial PbZrO3 thin films on silicon by leveraging thermal tensile-strain engineering, achieving near-zero remanent polarization, nanosecond switching, and large reversible electrostrain for high-performance nanoelectronics.
AI.motivation: Antiferroelectrics offer promise for nanoelectronics but suffer from limited domain control and incompatibility with silicon-based devices due to structural/chemical mismatches of conventional oxide platforms.
AI.method: Thermal tensile-strain engineering converts thermal mismatch into a functional advantage to grow epitaxial PbZrO3 thin films on silicon, achieving a tensile strain regime unattainable on conventional perovskite substrates. Combined theoretical and experimental studies were performed.
AI.result: Tensile strain stabilizes the (004)o domain enabling direct one-step switching (vs. compressive-strain-stabilized (240)o domains switching through intermediate ferrielectric states). Films exhibit near-zero remanent polarization, square double hysteresis, ~75ns switching, ~0.6% reversible electrostrain, and robust operation windows.
AI.conclusion: Domain-engineered ideal antiferroelectricity on silicon opens a viable route toward high-performance antiferroelectric nano-electronic devices.

title: Electron Delocalization versus Emission Coherence of Quantum Dot Superlattices
summary: Cooperative emission is a collective quantum optical process that requires macroscopic phase coherence among coupled emitters. Recent observations of cooperative emission in QD superlattices have renewed interest in how such coherence emerges in nanostructured solids. Meanwhile, theoretical studies have long discussed the relationship between electronic delocalization and coherence, particularly whether delocalized states necessarily give rise to cooperative emission. This study addresses this question through power-dependent steady-state PL and time-resolved PL decay measurements. The findings indicate that, although the quantum resonance peak exhibits delocalized excitonic characteristics, it shows no signatures of cooperative radiation. In particular, neither superlinear intensity scaling nor power-dependent emission delay was observed, indicating the absence of cooperative-radiation signatures. This can be understood from two disorder-related aspects. Temperature-dependent spectroscopy reveals pronounced inhomogeneous broadening and low-temperature dark-exciton participation, pointing to intra-domain static disorder and exciton-state mixing. These effects collectively hinder the establishment of macroscopic coherence. The temperature dependence of the quantum resonance peak decay lifetime is consistent with two-dimensional exciton dynamics. This work provides direct experimental evidence that electronic delocalization can be decoupled from cooperative coherence in CdSe quantum dot superlattices.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that electronic delocalization in CdSe quantum dot superlattices does not automatically lead to cooperative emission; disorder-induced inhomogeneous broadening and dark-exciton participation prevent macroscopic coherence despite delocalized excitonic states.
AI.motivation: To resolve the theoretical debate on whether delocalized electronic states necessarily produce cooperative (superradiant) emission in nanostructured solids, particularly in QD superlattices where recent observations have renewed interest.
AI.method: Power-dependent steady-state photoluminescence (PL) and time-resolved PL decay measurements, combined with temperature-dependent spectroscopy, on CdSe quantum dot superlattices.
AI.result: No superlinear intensity scaling or power-dependent emission delay was observed, indicating no cooperative radiation. The quantum resonance peak shows delocalized excitonic character but no cooperative signatures. Temperature dependence reveals inhomogeneous broadening and low-temperature dark-exciton participation.
AI.conclusion: Electronic delocalization can be decoupled from cooperative coherence in CdSe QD superlattices; intra-domain static disorder and exciton-state mixing collectively hinder the establishment of macroscopic phase coherence.

title: A Field-Theoretic Framework for Work Statistics and Universal Scaling in Non-equilibrium Phase Transitions
summary: We develop a field-theoretic framework for work statistics in $O(N)$ models driven through criticality. By analyzing the dynamic renormalization group flow of composite power operators, we find the Kibble-Zurek scaling laws as a natural consequence of the flow, and we derive the scaling of work cumulants relevant to Kibble-Zurek scaling of topological defects from first principles, bypassing heuristic freeze-out argument. This yields the universal scaling $c_n \sim τ_Q^{-α_n}$ for the $n$-th work cumulant density: isolated quantum systems exhibit a scaling of $α_n = p(d+nz)ν/(1+pzν)$, whereas open quantum and classical systems undergo a dimensional collapse to $α_n = pdν/(1+pzν)$. Validated by exact Gaussian solutions and numerical simulations, our theory establishes a foundation for general work statistics far from equilibrium, thereby bridging stochastic thermodynamics and the renormalization group theory.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a field-theoretic framework using dynamic renormalization group theory to derive universal scaling laws for work statistics in O(N) models driven through criticality, revealing distinct scaling exponents for isolated vs. open/classical systems and establishing a bridge between stochastic thermodynamics and RG theory.
AI.motivation: To provide a first-principles derivation of Kibble-Zurek scaling laws for work cumulants in critical O(N) models, bypassing heuristic freeze-out arguments, and to unify stochastic thermodynamics with renormalization group theory.
AI.method: A field-theoretic framework analyzing dynamic renormalization group flow of composite power operators to derive work statistics in O(N) models driven through criticality.
AI.result: Universal scaling $c_n \sim τ_Q^{-α_n}$ for the $n$-th work cumulant density, where isolated quantum systems yield $α_n = p(d+nz)ν/(1+pzν)$ and open/classical systems exhibit dimensional collapse to $α_n = pdν/(1+pzν)$. Results validated by exact Gaussian solutions and numerical simulations.
AI.conclusion: The theory establishes a rigorous foundation for general work statistics far from equilibrium and bridges stochastic thermodynamics with renormalization group theory.

title: Learning Inhomogeneous Heisenberg Hamiltonians in Nanographene Spin Chains
summary: Inferring microscopic Hamiltonians from experimental data is a central challenge in quantum materials and quantum simulation. In low-dimensional spin systems, exchange interactions are often assumed to be spatially uniform, despite structural and environmental inhomogeneities that can locally modify the coupling. Here, we leverage a local, length-independent machine learning methodology to reconstruct spatially modulated exchange interactions directly from inelastic scanning tunneling spectroscopy maps. We demonstrate this approach with nanographene spin chains, identifying both near-uniform and inhomogeneous regimes across the synthesized magnets. The reconstructed models quantitatively reproduce the experimental spectra and recover the correct scaling of the excitation gap with system size. Our results establish a general strategy to bridge local spectroscopic measurements with effective many-body Hamiltonians.

AI.tldr: A machine learning method reconstructs spatially modulated exchange interactions in quantum spin chains directly from scanning tunneling spectroscopy maps, demonstrated on nanographene spin chains, recovering both uniform and inhomogeneous regimes with quantitative accuracy.
AI.motivation: Inferring microscopic Hamiltonians from experimental data is challenging; exchange interactions in low-dimensional spin systems are often assumed uniform despite structural inhomogeneities that locally modify coupling.
AI.method: A local, length-independent machine learning methodology reconstructs spatially modulated exchange interactions directly from inelastic scanning tunneling spectroscopy maps.
AI.result: Applied to nanographene spin chains, identifying near-uniform and inhomogeneous regimes; reconstructed models quantitatively reproduce experimental spectra and recover correct excitation gap scaling with system size.
AI.conclusion: Establishes a general strategy to bridge local spectroscopic measurements with effective many-body Hamiltonians.

title: Why can genetic algorithms work in high-dimensional search spaces?
summary: We show that the effective dynamics of the elitist $(1+M)$ genetic algorithm is, in the limit of small mutations, clipped gradient descent on the loss in the presence of anisotropic Gaussian white noise. In expectation, therefore, a simple mutation-selection genetic algorithm follows the gradient of the loss, without explicit calculation of gradients and without averaging over loss evaluations. The genetic algorithm is slower than gradient descent because of the noise that acts in directions transverse to the gradient. However, this slowdown is controlled not by the number of parameters of the search space but by the effective rank of the Hessian of the loss function. For the concentrated Hessian spectra observed in neural-network loss functions the effective rank can be far smaller than the number of parameters, which may explain why genetic algorithms can scale to large search spaces.

AI.tldr: The elitist (1+M) genetic algorithm with small mutations performs clipped gradient descent under anisotropic Gaussian noise, slowing down only according to the effective rank of the loss Hessian, not parameter count—helping explain GA scalability in large neural network search spaces.
AI.motivation: To understand why genetic algorithms can scale to large search spaces (like neural networks) despite lacking explicit gradient calculations, by analyzing their effective dynamics.
AI.method: Theoretical analysis showing that in the small-mutation limit, the elitist (1+M) GA's effective dynamics correspond to clipped gradient descent with anisotropic Gaussian white noise.
AI.result: The GA follows the gradient in expectation without computing gradients; noise acts in transverse directions; the slowdown is bounded by the effective rank of the loss Hessian, which is often much smaller than the number of parameters for neural-network losses.
AI.conclusion: The effective rank of the Hessian, not parameter dimensionality, controls GA slowdown, providing a theoretical explanation for GA scalability in high-dimensional neural network optimization.

title: Ferromagnetic ordering in Hubbard models
summary:
One of the long-standing and only partially solved problems of theoretical condensed matter physics and mathematical physics is to demonstrate that ground states of some of the versions of the Hubbard model can exhibit a ferromagnetic ordering. It has long been speculated that the opportunity crucial for the occurrence of ferromagnetism is the structure of the lattice on which the Hubbard model is formulated \cite{TasakiMB}. As a consequence, while on simple cubic lattices no ferromagnetic ordering seems to be possible, it can naturally arise, even for low densities of magnetic moment carriers, on so-called frustrated lattices.
  We investigate the problem of ground state ferromagnetic ordering with the use of the formula for ground-state energy of interacting fermions as the first term of `density expansion', proven rigorously by Lieb, Seiringer and Solovej \cite{fermi exact} in continuum and by Giuliani \cite{hub exact} for the simple cubic lattice. Assuming that analogous expansion holds also for certain another lattices we apply this formula to five frustrated lattices -- among them to the face-centered cubic one. The hypothesis is confirmed: most of examined models formulated on frustrated lattices do indeed have ferromagnetic ground states already for densities being moderate or even low. Although the approach adopted cannot be treated as a rigorous proof that the ground state is ferromagnetic, the results obtained here strongly indicate that it can be the case. Moreover, as in some cases FM occurs at low densities, one can hope that it would be possible to prove convergence of the density expansion and prove rigorously the occurrence of `wealthy ferromagnetism' in these cases.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates ground-state ferromagnetism in the Hubbard model on frustrated lattices (including face-centered cubic) using a density expansion formula, finding strong evidence that ferromagnetic ordering occurs even at low to moderate densities, though the approach is not a rigorous proof.
AI.motivation: To address the long-standing problem of demonstrating ferromagnetic ordering in ground states of the Hubbard model, and to test the hypothesis that the lattice structure (specifically frustrated lattices) is crucial for the occurrence of ferromagnetism.
AI.method: Apply the Lieb-Seiringer-Solovej density expansion formula for ground-state energy of interacting fermions (originally proven in continuum and for simple cubic lattices) to five frustrated lattices, including the face-centered cubic lattice, assuming the expansion holds for these lattices as well.
AI.result: Most models formulated on frustrated lattices exhibit ferromagnetic ground states already at moderate or even low densities. The results strongly indicate ferromagnetic ordering, though they do not constitute a rigorous proof.
AI.conclusion: The hypothesis is confirmed: frustrated lattices enable ferromagnetic ordering in the Hubbard model. The occurrence of ferromagnetism at low densities suggests potential for proving convergence of the density expansion and rigorously establishing "wealthy ferromagnetism" in these cases.

title: Strain-Driven Domain Walls in Antiferromagnets
summary: We derive an equation describing domain wall motion in antiferromagnets under the influence of normal strain. From this equation, we find that the domain wall moves towards positions where $\varepsilon_{xx}$ is high and $\varepsilon_{zz}$ is low. Furthermore, each strain component leads to a different terminal velocity for the same strain profile. This difference arises because both strains affect the domain wall width in opposite ways: $\varepsilon_{xx}$ reduces the width, whereas $\varepsilon_{zz}$ increases it. The model is then compared with mumax$^+$ simulations for various strain profiles, including a strain gradient, an oscillating strain, and a Rayleigh wave. The comparison shows good agreement between the analytical and numerical results. Finally, we demonstrate the potential of standing surface acoustic waves as an error correction method in racetrack memory.

AI.tldr: The paper derives an equation for domain wall motion in antiferromagnets under normal strain, finding that walls move toward high εxx and low εzz due to opposite effects on wall width. Analytical results match mumax+ simulations for various strain profiles, and standing surface acoustic waves are proposed for error correction in racetrack memory.
AI.motivation: To understand and model domain wall motion in antiferromagnets under normal strain, and explore its potential application for error correction in racetrack memory.
AI.method: Derivation of an analytical equation for domain wall motion under strain, validated by mumax+ micromagnetic simulations for strain gradients, oscillating strain, and Rayleigh waves.
AI.result: Domain walls move toward high εxx and low εzz; εxx reduces domain wall width while εzz increases it, leading to different terminal velocities. Analytical and numerical results show good agreement.
AI.conclusion: Standing surface acoustic waves show promise as an error correction method in racetrack memory devices.

title: Emergent energy scales in magnonic systems with relative motion
summary: Relative motion between interacting systems can generate emergent energy scales that are absent in isolated systems. While uniform motion can be eliminated by a Galilean transformation, relative motion between interacting systems generally cannot. In the presence of characteristic spatial structures, relative motion gives rise to a Doppler frequency scale determined by the characteristic wavevector of the excitation and the relative velocity of the system. This emergent scale provides a fundamental mechanism for driving nonequilibrium phenomena in moving systems. In particular, the emergent energy scale is determined by how the relative motion probes the spatial structure of the relevant excitation. In this tutorial, we illustrate these ideas using magnonic systems as a concrete platform. We first discuss motion-induced magnon transport between relatively moving ferromagnets, in which the Doppler frequency serves as an effective nonequilibrium bias in the perturbative regime. This mechanism produces magnon currents even in the absence of conventional driving forces such as temperature gradients or chemical potential differences. We then introduce motion-induced parametric instabilities. When the emergent scale becomes sufficiently large to resonantly create magnon pairs, the perturbative description breaks down, and the magnonic vacuum becomes unstable. Above a critical velocity threshold, spontaneous magnon-pair creation emerges, resulting in strongly enhanced transport and nonequilibrium dynamics. Connections to related phenomena, including quantum friction, Cherenkov emission, and Zeldovich superradiance, are also highlighted. The concept of an emergent energy scale provides a unifying framework for understanding transport phenomena and instabilities in quantum systems with relative motion.

AI.tldr: This tutorial introduces the concept of an emergent energy scale arising from relative motion between interacting systems, using magnonic systems as a platform. It covers motion-induced magnon transport (Doppler bias driving currents without temperature gradients) and motion-induced parametric instabilities (where above a critical velocity, spontaneous magnon-pair creation occurs). Connections to quantum friction, Cherenkov emission, and Zeldovich superradiance are discussed.
AI.motivation: Relative motion between interacting systems generates emergent energy scales absent in isolated systems. While uniform motion can be removed by Galilean transformation, relative motion with spatial structures creates a Doppler frequency scale that fundamentally drives nonequilibrium phenomena, providing a unifying framework for understanding transport and instabilities.
AI.method: The paper uses magnonic systems as a concrete platform, analyzing motion-induced magnon transport in the perturbative regime (where Doppler frequency acts as an effective nonequilibrium bias) and motion-induced parametric instabilities (where the emergent scale resonantly creates magnon pairs, breaking perturbative descriptions).
AI.result: The Doppler frequency from relative motion produces magnon currents without conventional driving forces (temperature gradients or chemical potential differences). Above a critical velocity threshold, spontaneous magnon-pair creation occurs, leading to strongly enhanced transport and nonequilibrium dynamics.
AI.conclusion: The emergent energy scale from relative motion provides a unifying framework for understanding transport phenomena and instabilities in quantum systems with relative motion, with connections to quantum friction, Cherenkov emission, and Zeldovich superradiance.

title: Bilinear Flexo-Antiferrodistortive Coupling in Ferroelastics: Polar Twins, Antiphase Boundaries and Fingerprints of Alterelectricity
comment: 21 pages, including 4 figures and Supplementary Materials
summary: Using the Landau-Ginsburg-Devonshire approach we show that the linear gradient-type coupling between the electric polarization vector and antiferrodistortive long-range order parameter pseudovector, that has the form of Lifshitz invariant and named "bilinear flexo-antiferrodistortive coupling", can emerge in all antiferrodistortive ferroelastics, since it is symmetry-allowed. Using the four sublattices model we reveal that the bilinear flexo-antiferrodistortive coupling can induce the sublattice-sensitive polarization at the twin walls and antiphase boundaries in antiferrodistortive ferroelastics without any ferroelectric or antiferroelectric ordering. Since the induced polarization is perpendicular to the antiferrodistortive long-range order parameter and counter-directed in neighboring sublattices with checkerboard-type direction of antiferrodistortive long-range order parameter, such structure of polarization may correspond to the alterelectric-type quadrupolar electric order. However, physical manifestations of the bilinear flexo-antiferrodistortive coupling are invisible in most nanostructured antiferrodistortive ferroelectrics and antiferroelectrics due to the domination of piezoelectric and/or linear flexoelectric couplings. Since a common flexoelectric coupling cannot induce the alterelectric-type polarization at domain boundaries in antiferrodistortive ferroelastics, we believe that the bilinear flexo-antiferrodistortive coupling can be a fingerprint of recently discovered alterelectric long-range order in antiferrodistortive ferroelastics.

AI.tldr: This paper reveals a bilinear flexo-antiferrodistortive coupling (Lifshitz invariant) symmetry-allowed in all antiferrodistortive ferroelastics, which induces sublattice-sensitive polarization at domain boundaries without ferroelectric/antiferroelectric ordering, potentially corresponding to alterelectric-type quadrupolar order, and is proposed as a fingerprint of alterelectric long-range order.
AI.motivation: To identify and characterize a previously overlooked bilinear gradient-type coupling (flexo-antiferrodistortive coupling) in antiferrodistortive materials and explore its ability to induce polarization without ferroelectric or antiferroelectric ordering, particularly its connection to alterelectric order.
AI.method: Landau-Ginsburg-Devonshire phenomenological approach combined with a four-sublattice model to analyze symmetry-allowed couplings and predict polarization structures at twin walls and antiphase boundaries.
AI.result: The bilinear flexo-antiferrodistortive coupling induces sublattice-sensitive polarization perpendicular to the antiferrodistortive order parameter with a checkerboard pattern, consistent with alterelectric-type quadrupolar electric order; however, its manifestations are masked by piezoelectric and flexoelectric couplings in most nanostructured antiferrodistortive ferroelectrics/antiferroelectrics.
AI.conclusion: The bilinear flexo-antiferrodistortive coupling serves as a distinct fingerprint of alterelectric long-range order in antiferrodistortive ferroelastics, as common flexoelectric coupling cannot produce such alterelectric-type polarization.

title: Quantum Theory of Current-Generating Local Orbital Magnetization
summary: Local orbital magnetization is the field whose rotation generates the equilibrium current density. Unlike spin magnetization, a quantum-mechanical local formula consistent with both this current relation and the modern theory of bulk orbital magnetization has been missing. In this work, we derive a quantum-mechanical formula for the local orbital magnetization for non-interacting electrons by considering local-flux response of the grand potential. The local-flux response fixes the formula uniquely in two dimensions, whereas in three dimensions it selects a natural representative within a longitudinal ambiguity. Furthermore, coarse graining yields a natural local marker that generates the current to third-derivative order, and its site-position moment equals the orbital magnetic quadrupole moment of finite-size systems. We illustrate the obtained results with the Haldane model.

AI.tldr: Derives a quantum-mechanical formula for local orbital magnetization consistent with current density and modern bulk theory, resolving a long-standing gap.
AI.motivation: A quantum-mechanical local formula for orbital magnetization that satisfies both the current relation (local magnetization as the generator of equilibrium current via rotation) and the modern theory of bulk orbital magnetization has been missing.
AI.method: Derives the local orbital magnetization formula via local-flux response of the grand potential for non-interacting electrons. In 2D the formula is uniquely fixed; in 3D a natural representative is selected within a longitudinal ambiguity. Coarse graining yields a local marker generating current to third-derivative order.
AI.result: The local-flux response uniquely determines the formula in 2D and selects a natural representative in 3D. The coarse-grained marker generates current up to third-derivative order, and its site-position moment equals the orbital magnetic quadrupole moment. Illustrated with the Haldane model.
AI.conclusion: Provides the missing quantum-mechanical local orbital magnetization formula that is consistent with both equilibrium current generation and the modern theory of bulk orbital magnetization.

title: Optimizing Expert-Designed Crystal Graph Networks for Band-Gap Prediction with an Autonomous LLM Research Loop
summary: Predicting a material's properties from its structure is a central, fast-advancing problem in computational materials science. A decade of work has produced standard public benchmarks and many published machine-learning models for the task (Dunn et al., 2020). The task's fixed metric and these baselines make it a natural setting for autonomous agent research (Karpathy, 2026). On the MatBench band-gap benchmark ($>$100k crystals), a general-purpose coding agent autonomously built the most accurate model trained without external pretraining, ahead of all seventeen expert-designed models reported for the task. A closer analysis shows it reached this by implementing known methods: either already standard in crystal neural-network models, or borrowed from other areas of machine learning. The contributing implementations include element-pair features on each message-passing edge and a crystal space-group embedding. The work not only demonstrates that LLM-agent autonomous research can optimize an expert-designed machine learning model for material property prediction, but also investigates the limitations of such autonomous research.

AI.tldr: A general-purpose coding agent autonomously built the best-performing model on the MatBench band-gap benchmark by implementing known methods like element-pair edge features and space-group embeddings, outperforming all 17 expert-designed models.
AI.motivation: To explore whether LLM-based autonomous agents can optimize machine learning models for materials property prediction, and to investigate the limitations of such autonomous research.
AI.method: A general-purpose coding agent was deployed on the MatBench band-gap benchmark (>100k crystals). It autonomously implemented element-pair features on message-passing edges and crystal space-group embeddings, combining standard crystal network techniques with methods borrowed from other ML domains.
AI.result: The agent produced the most accurate model trained without external pretraining, surpassing all 17 expert-designed baselines on the MatBench band-gap benchmark.
AI.conclusion: LLM-agent autonomous research can optimize expert-designed models for material property prediction, but the approach has limitations—the agent succeeded by recombining known methods rather than inventing novel architectures.

title: Probing Quantum Geometric Phases via Scanning Tunneling Microscopy
summary: The quantum geometric phase intrinsically dictates the geometry, topology, and many-body correlations of electronic wave functions. While quantum geometric phases are conventionally inferred through momentum-space probes or macroscopic transport measurements, their direct visualization and quantification in real space have historically been restricted by the spatial averaging of bulk techniques. Scanning tunneling microscopy and spectroscopy (STM/STS) circumvent this limitation, leveraging atomic-scale spatial resolution and high energy sensitivity to resolve local electronic phase profiles directly. This review highlights recent progress across four representative methodologies: probing the Aharonov-Bohm (AB) geometric phase via nanoscale real space interferometry; extracting the Berry phase from defect-induced quasiparticle interference and wavefront dislocations; reconstructing the complex phase structure in symmetric systems, such as magic-angle graphene, using order parameter decomposition; and mapping the phase textures and topological defects of pair density wave (PDW) and charge density wave (CDW) in unconventional superconductors utilizing the numerical 2D lock-in technique. Together, these developments show how quantum phases can be translated onto real space and locally resolvable observables. Phase-resolved STM imaging provides stringent constraints on topological states of matter, symmetry-breaking patterns, and strong electronic correlations, outlining a robust framework for in situ phase engineering in quantum materials.

AI.tldr: This review highlights how quantum geometric phases—traditionally measured via momentum-space or bulk transport—can now be directly visualized and quantified in real space using STM/STS, covering four key methodologies: Aharonov-Bohm interferometry, Berry phase extraction from quasiparticle interference, complex phase reconstruction in symmetric systems (e.g., magic-angle graphene), and mapping phase textures in PDW/CDW systems via lock-in techniques. These advances enable in situ phase engineering and provide stringent constraints on topological states, symmetry-breaking, and strong correlations.
AI.motivation: Quantum geometric phases are fundamental to wave function geometry, topology, and many-body correlations, but their direct real-space visualization has been limited by spatial averaging in bulk techniques. The motivation is to overcome this limitation using STM/STS, which offers atomic-scale spatial resolution and high energy sensitivity to resolve local electronic phase profiles.
AI.method: The review summarizes four representative STM/STS-based methodologies: (1) Aharonov-Bohm geometric phase probing via nanoscale real-space interferometry; (2) Berry phase extraction from defect-induced quasiparticle interference and wavefront dislocations; (3) complex phase structure reconstruction in symmetric systems (e.g., magic-angle graphene) using order parameter decomposition; and (4) mapping phase textures and topological defects of pair density wave (PDW) and charge density wave (CDW) in unconventional superconductors using a numerical 2D lock-in technique.
AI.result: These methods collectively translate quantum phases onto real-space, locally resolvable observables, enabling stringent constraints on topological states of matter, symmetry-breaking patterns, and strong electronic correlations.
AI.conclusion: Phase-resolved STM imaging provides a robust framework for in situ phase engineering in quantum materials, directly linking quantum geometric phases to real-space measurements.

title: Length--Velocity Gauge Equivalence of Quantum Geometric Nonlinear Conductivity
comment: The manuscript contains 8 pages of main text with 2 figures, plus 14 pages of appendices
summary: Nonlinear transport has emerged as a sensitive probe of quantum geometry beyond the Berry-curvature physics of linear response. However, the intrinsic second-order dc response remains conceptually subtle: different quantum and semiclassical formulations can appear to give different static limits, with different assignments of Fermi sea and Fermi surface contributions. Here we resolve this ambiguity by developing a gauge-consistent density-matrix theory of intrinsic nonlinear conductivity in both the length gauge, where the electric field couples through the position operator, and the velocity gauge, where it enters through the vector potential. We show that the two gauges give the same adiabatic dc response when the same retarded continuation is used for all external frequencies and when the velocity gauge current includes all field-dependent vertices. The apparent Fermi sea terms cancel in the full expression, leaving a Fermi surface quantum geometric contribution determined by the band-normalized quantum metric. This result implies that a fully gapped insulator has no residual dc nonlinear Hall current in the adiabatic clean limit. The reactive part of the Fermi surface term agrees with the original semiclassical Berry-connection-polarizability response, while the dissipative Ohmic sector requires a more careful treatment of relaxation and impurity scattering. Our work establishes the length-velocity gauge equivalence for quantum geometric nonlinear response and provides a foundation for using nonlinear transport to probe magnetic quantum geometry, especially in PT-symmetric antiferromagnets.

AI.tldr: The paper resolves ambiguities in nonlinear transport theory by proving gauge equivalence between length and velocity gauge formulations, showing that intrinsic second-order dc response is purely a Fermi surface quantum geometric effect (not Fermi sea), and that the apparent Fermi sea terms cancel, leaving contributions determined by the band-normalized quantum metric.
AI.motivation: Nonlinear transport can probe quantum geometry beyond Berry-curvature physics of linear response, but the intrinsic second-order dc response has been conceptually subtle with different formulations giving different static limits and ambiguous assignments of Fermi sea vs. Fermi surface contributions.
AI.method: The authors develop a gauge-consistent density-matrix theory of intrinsic nonlinear conductivity in both the length gauge (electric field couples via position operator) and velocity gauge (via vector potential), ensuring the same retarded continuation for all external frequencies and including all field-dependent vertices.
AI.result: The two gauges yield identical adiabatic dc response when consistently treated. Apparent Fermi sea terms cancel, leaving a Fermi surface contribution determined by the band-normalized quantum metric. A fully gapped insulator has no residual dc nonlinear Hall current in the adiabatic clean limit. The reactive part matches the semiclassical Berry-connection-polarizability response, while the dissipative sector requires relaxation/impurity treatment.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes length-velocity gauge equivalence for quantum geometric nonlinear response and provides a foundation for using nonlinear transport to probe magnetic quantum geometry, especially in PT-symmetric antiferromagnets.

title: The substitutional atomic distance model for predicting lattice thermal conductivity in alloys
summary: Understanding phonon transport in alloys is crucial for the design of high-performance electronic and thermoelectric devices. However, conventional theoretical models fail to provide a clear physical picture of phonon scattering caused by atomic disorder in alloys, and their prediction accuracy is limited. In this work, a new substitutional atomic distance model for alloys is proposed, providing an intuitive physical picture. SiGe and InGaAs alloys are taken as representative systems, and their thermal conductivities are calculated, showing good agreement with previous experimental measurements. The results indicate that alloy scattering plays a dominant role in reducing thermal conductivity. This study provides new insights into phonon transport in alloys and offers guidance for tailoring thermal properties through compositional engineering.

AI.tldr: A new substitutional atomic distance model is proposed for alloys to better understand phonon transport, validated on SiGe and InGaAs systems, showing good agreement with experiments and highlighting alloy scattering's dominant role in reducing thermal conductivity.
AI.motivation: Conventional theoretical models fail to provide a clear physical picture of phonon scattering caused by atomic disorder in alloys, and their prediction accuracy is limited.
AI.method: A new substitutional atomic distance model for alloys is proposed, providing an intuitive physical picture; thermal conductivities of SiGe and InGaAs alloys are calculated.
AI.result: The model shows good agreement with previous experimental measurements; alloy scattering plays a dominant role in reducing thermal conductivity.
AI.conclusion: This study provides new insights into phonon transport in alloys and offers guidance for tailoring thermal properties through compositional engineering.

title: Spin-1 Dirac dispersion and Chern insulating phases in 2D honeycomb Sierpiński fractal
summary: Graphene-based Sierpiński fractals host a zero-energy chiral mode and spin-1 Dirac dispersions within the nearest-neighbor tight-binding model. However, the presence of complex next-nearest neighbor hopping arising from the local flux and the staggered Semenoff mass terms, modeled within the Haldane Hamiltonian, breaks the time-reversal and spatial inversion symmetries, respectively, and makes these flat bands dispersive. Moreover, they introduce rich topological phases in this class of systems that can be characterized by Chern numbers up to $\pm 3$, i.e., beyond the conventional honeycomb lattice. These observations pave the way for the exploration of 2D periodic fractals beyond graphene, where topological phase transitions can be realized through externally applied fields.

AI.tldr: Graphene-based Sierpiński fractals host zero-energy chiral modes and spin-1 Dirac dispersions under nearest-neighbor hopping. Adding next-nearest neighbor hopping and mass terms (Haldane model) breaks symmetries, makes flat bands dispersive, and introduces topological phases with Chern numbers up to ±3, beyond conventional honeycomb lattices. This enables topological phase transitions in 2D periodic fractals via external fields.
AI.motivation: To explore topological phases in graphene-based Sierpiński fractals beyond the simple nearest-neighbor tight-binding model, specifically investigating how symmetry-breaking terms (next-nearest neighbor hopping, staggered mass) induce richer topological behavior with higher Chern numbers.
AI.method: The Haldane Hamiltonian is employed to model next-nearest neighbor hopping (breaking time-reversal symmetry via local flux) and staggered Semenoff mass (breaking spatial inversion symmetry) on graphene-based Sierpiński fractal lattices. Chern numbers are computed to characterize topological phases.
AI.result: Symmetry-breaking terms make originally flat bands dispersive and introduce topological phases characterized by Chern numbers up to ±3, exceeding the maximum Chern number (±1) found in conventional honeycomb lattices.
AI.conclusion: 2D periodic fractals beyond graphene can host rich topological phases and phase transitions tunable by external fields, opening new avenues for topological fractal materials.

title: Ferron Hall effect: Transverse accumulation of polarization driven by thermal gradients in ferroelectrics
summary: The phonon Hall effect describes the generation of a transverse heat current in response to a longitudinal thermal gradient in a magnetic field. Here, we theoretically demonstrate that, when the lattice excitations deflected by the Hall effect carry electric dipole moments, their transverse motion produces an accumulation of electric polarization in ferroelectric materials. This accumulation is driven by lattice excitations that carry polarization, known as ferrons, and we therefore call the mechanism the ferron Hall effect. Using atomistic lattice dynamics with parameters obtained from density functional theory, we illustrate the effect in the prototypical ferroelectric BaTiO3. Our results identify ferrons as the electric-polarization analogues of magnons in transverse transport and provide a route toward thermal and magnetic manipulation of ferroic order.

AI.tldr: The paper theoretically demonstrates the ferron Hall effect, where lattice excitations (ferrons) carrying electric dipole moments are deflected by the phonon Hall effect, accumulating electric polarization in ferroelectric materials. Using BaTiO₃ as an example, it identifies ferrons as electric-polarization analogues of magnons in transverse transport.
AI.motivation: To extend the phonon Hall effect concept to ferroelectric materials, where lattice excitations carry not only heat but also electric dipole moments, enabling electric polarization accumulation via transverse transport.
AI.method: Atomistic lattice dynamics with parameters obtained from density functional theory (DFT), applied to the prototypical ferroelectric BaTiO₃.
AI.result: When lattice excitations (ferrons) are deflected by the phonon Hall effect, their transverse motion accumulates electric polarization in ferroelectric materials.
AI.conclusion: Ferrons serve as electric-polarization analogues of magnons in transverse transport, offering a route toward thermal and magnetic manipulation of ferroic order.

title: Hall viscosity from metric-sensitive dichroic probes
summary: Hall viscosity characterizes the geometric response of a quantum Hall droplet to deformations of the underlying metric, yet it has remained difficult to measure directly. We propose a spectroscopic probe based on circular dichroism, using chiral metric-sensitive drives -- implemented as rotating quadrupolar ("saddle") perturbations -- that effectively modulate the metric and couple to the generators of area-preserving deformations. The resulting dichroic signal directly measures the Hall viscosity, while frequency-resolved spectroscopy disentangles it from other excitations. A local formulation further enables spatially resolved markers of Hall viscosity applicable to both continuum and lattice systems. Our results open a direct route to measuring Hall viscosity in quantum-engineered platforms such as cold atoms in optical lattices.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a spectroscopic probe using chiral, metric-sensitive drives (rotating quadrupolar perturbations) to directly measure Hall viscosity in quantum Hall droplets via circular dichroism, with frequency and spatial resolution applicable to both continuum and lattice systems.
AI.motivation: Hall viscosity characterizes geometric response of quantum Hall droplets to metric deformations but has remained difficult to measure directly.
AI.method: Proposes spectroscopic probe based on circular dichroism using rotating quadrupolar ("saddle") perturbations that modulate the metric and couple to area-preserving deformations, with a local formulation for spatially resolved markers.
AI.result: Dichroic signal directly measures Hall viscosity; frequency-resolved spectroscopy disentangles it from other excitations.
AI.conclusion: Opens a direct route to measuring Hall viscosity in quantum-engineered platforms such as cold atoms in optical lattices.

title: Field-induced topological Hall effect and butterfly-shaped magnetoresistance in the centrosymmetric antiferromagnet EuAuAs
summary: The coupling between magnetic and electronic degrees of freedom gives rise to a variety of intriguing transport phenomena. Among them, the topological Hall effect, originating from the real-space Berry phase associated with nontrivial magnetic textures, has attracted considerable attention. Here, we systematically investigate the magnetic and transport properties of antiferromagnet EuAuAs. Magnetic characterizations reveal antiferromagnetic transition at 5.7 K and 6.3 K for $H \parallel ab$ and $H \parallel c$, accompanied by metamagnetic transition and small hysteresis for $H \parallel ab$. Electrical transport measurements reveal a pronounced topological Hall effct in the antiferromagnetic state with $H \parallel ab$ and $I \parallel c$, which may be attributed to finite scalar spin chirality. Furthermore, the magnetoresistance exhibits butterfly-shaped hysteresis and strong angular dependence, which are likely associated with spin-dependent electron scattering, magnetic-domain evolution, and domain-wall pinning. Our results suggest that field-induced spin textures play an important role in the magnetotransport properties and provide insights into the interplay between magnetic textures and electronic transport in centrosymmetric antiferromagnets.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates the antiferromagnet EuAuAs, revealing a topological Hall effect in its antiferromagnetic state, along with butterfly-shaped magnetoresistance hysteresis and strong angular dependence, attributed to field-induced spin textures and scalar spin chirality.
AI.motivation: To understand the coupling between magnetic and electronic degrees of freedom, particularly the topological Hall effect arising from nontrivial magnetic textures, and to explore magnetotransport in centrosymmetric antiferromagnets.
AI.method: Systematic magnetic characterization (magnetization measurements under H ∥ ab and H ∥ c) and electrical transport measurements (topological Hall effect, magnetoresistance, angular dependence) on single-crystal EuAuAs.
AI.result: Antiferromagnetic transitions at 5.7 K (H ∥ ab) and 6.3 K (H ∥ c); metamagnetic transition with small hysteresis for H ∥ ab; pronounced topological Hall effect in the antiferromagnetic state (H ∥ ab, I ∥ c); butterfly-shaped magnetoresistance hysteresis with strong angular dependence.
AI.conclusion: Field-induced spin textures play a crucial role in magnetotransport properties, and the results provide insights into the interplay between magnetic textures and electronic transport in centrosymmetric antiferromagnets.

title: Perfect elliptic dichroism: Probing the metric of anisotropic quantum Hall droplets
summary: Understanding the geometry of quantum Hall systems is a central challenge in modern condensed matter physics. We introduce a framework for probing the geometric structure of quantum Hall droplets by engineering the geometry of a dichroic probe and identifying the onset of "perfect elliptic dichroism", a regime in which the system responds exclusively to an elliptically polarized drive of a given chirality. This phenomenon provides a direct diagnostic of the droplet's intrinsic metric, and we show that it extends naturally to ideal Chern bands, where holomorphicity of the occupied states guarantees the vanishing of one chiral absorption rate with a quantized response for the other. In lattice realizations, such as the Harper-Hofstadter model, finite lattice-spacing corrections break the exact continuum metric description and give rise to a renormalized, emergent Landau-orbit metric; the probe ellipticity at which perfect dichroism is achieved then shifts accordingly, offering a direct spectroscopic window onto this lattice-induced geometric renormalization. Our results illuminate the rich geometric structure of quantum Hall phases and offer concrete pathways for observing these effects in quantum-engineered platforms.

title: Consistent transition model for Bi0.5Na0.5TiO3 from temperature-dependent structural and electrical properties
summary: BNT based solid solutions are promising parent materials for lead free dielectric capacitors, thanks to their high recoverable energy densities and breakdown strengths. However, the ambient temperature symmetry and high temperature phase evolution of BNT remain unclear. Crucially, structural transformations and electrical ordering are most often considered independently, hindering a coherent understanding of the BNT phase transition. In this work, we combine X ray diffraction, transmission electron microscopy, Raman spectroscopy, impedance spectroscopy, and high field polarization cycling to establish a unified picture of the structural and dielectric response of BNT. Based on these results, we propose a consistent transition model for BNT that reconciles previously conflicting interpretations. This integrated structure property study provides a rationale for developing high performance, lead free energy storage materials.

AI.method: X-ray diffraction, transmission electron microscopy, Raman spectroscopy, impedance spectroscopy, and high-field polarization cycling are combined to establish a unified picture of structural and dielectric response.

title: Anomalous Duffing mechanics of a suspended carbon nanotube quantum dot at ultrastrong coupling
summary: At cryogenic temperatures, suspended single-wall carbon nanotube quantum dots act both as prototypical quantum dots as well as high-quality factor mechanical resonators. Single-electron tunneling enables reaching an ultrastrong electron-vibron coupling regime, where the coupling parameter exceeds the vibration frequency. Due to the high quality factors, a strongly nonlinear Duffing response is easily reached. Here, we quantitatively study the Duffing response parameters of such a device and their relation to Coulomb blockade oscillation. At the edges of single-electron tunneling regions, a local increase of the Duffing parameter corresponding to a stiffening spring is observed. Size and approximate scaling of the effect agree with single-electron tunneling phenomena, which however should lead to softening spring behaviour. Possible causes of these puzzling results are discussed.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates the nonlinear Duffing response of suspended carbon nanotube quantum dot mechanical resonators at cryogenic temperatures, finding an unexpected stiffening spring effect at the edges of single-electron tunneling regions that contradicts the predicted softening behavior.
AI.motivation: To quantitatively study the Duffing response parameters of suspended single-wall carbon nanotube quantum dots and their relationship to Coulomb blockade oscillation, particularly to understand the unexpected stiffening spring behavior observed at the edges of single-electron tunneling regions.
AI.method: Experimental measurement of the Duffing response parameters in a suspended single-wall carbon nanotube quantum dot device operating in the ultrastrong electron-vibron coupling regime, with analysis of the spring constant modification at single-electron tunneling region edges.
AI.result: A local increase of the Duffing parameter (stiffening spring) is observed at the edges of single-electron tunneling regions, with size and approximate scaling consistent with single-electron tunneling phenomena, though theory predicts a softening spring behavior instead.
AI.conclusion: The observed stiffening spring effect contradicts the expected softening behavior from single-electron tunneling theory; possible causes are discussed but remain unexplained, highlighting a puzzle in the electron-vibron coupling physics of these devices.

title: Analytical approximations of dispersion laws and ultra-complex conductivity diagrams
summary: We study the probability of the emergence of ultra-complex conductivity diagrams in conductors that satisfy the tight-binding approximation and have the simple or body-centered cubic lattice. The presence of ultra-complex conductivity diagrams allows us to observe a number of highly nontrivial effects in strong magnetic fields, however, the probability of their emergence in a given substance is quite low. In the case of the simple or body-centered cubic lattice, the leading tight-binding approximation does not allow us to estimate this probability due to the peculiarities of the spectra in this situation. To estimate this probability, we use higher-order corrections to the leading approximation, which yield more accurate analytical expressions for the electron spectra.

Due to spectral peculiarities, the leading approximation cannot estimate this probability, so higher-order corrections are used to obtain more accurate electron spectra and enable estimation.
AI.motivation: The emergence of ultra-complex conductivity diagrams enables observation of highly nontrivial effects in strong magnetic fields, but their occurrence probability is low and cannot be estimated using the leading tight-binding approximation for simple or body-centered cubic lattices due to spectral peculiarities.
AI.method: Higher-order corrections beyond the leading tight-binding approximation are employed to derive more accurate analytical expressions for electron spectra, enabling probability estimation of ultra-complex conductivity diagrams in simple and body-centered cubic lattices.

AI.conclusion: Higher-order corrections to the tight-binding approximation are necessary and effective for estimating the low probability of ultra-complex conductivity diagrams in simple and body-centered cubic lattices, which are relevant for observing nontrivial effects in strong magnetic fields.

title: Rolling Two-Dimensional Collinear Magnets into Chiral Nanotubes with $p$-Wave Magnetism
summary: $p$-wave magnets are noncollinear compensated magnetic systems that exhibit nonrelativistic antisymmetric spin splitting in momentum space. Their odd-parity spin symmetry enables unconventional spintronic functionalities, including highly efficient charge-to-spin conversion via the Edelstein effect. An outstanding question is whether such magnetic phases can emerge from simple and broadly accessible magnetic building blocks rather than from intrinsically noncollinear magnetic orders. Here, we show that rolling two-dimensional collinear magnets -- ferromagnets, antiferromagnets, and altermagnets -- into nanotubes generates a rich spin-symmetry landscape controlled by curvature, chirality, and magnetic order. Remarkably, chiral nanotubes hosting radial or tangential coplanar spin textures generically realize $p$-wave magnetism irrespective of the underlying collinear parent phase. The emergent odd-parity spin symmetry manifests itself in both electronic and magnonic spectra through antisymmetric $p$-wave spin splitting. Our results establish magnetic nanotubes as a versatile platform for engineering unconventional $p$-wave magnetism and predict a nonrelativistic Edelstein response that exceeds conventional spin-orbit-driven charge-to-spin conversion by more than an order of magnitude.

AI.method: The authors show that rolling two-dimensional collinear magnets (ferromagnets, antiferromagnets, and altermagnets) into nanotubes generates p-wave magnetism through curvature, chirality, and magnetic order engineering, independent of the parent collinear phase.
AI.result: Chiral nanotubes with radial or tangential coplanar spin textures generically realize p-wave magnetism, exhibiting antisymmetric p-wave spin splitting in both electronic and magnonic spectra, and a predicted nonrelativistic Edelstein response exceeding conventional spin-orbit-driven charge-to-spin conversion by more than an order of magnitude.
AI.conclusion: Magnetic nanotubes serve as a versatile platform for engineering unconventional p-wave magnetism and enable highly efficient spintronic functionalities.

title: Transport in extended Kitaev chain with time reversal symmetry breaking and long-range interaction
summary: We consider a junction consisting of an extended one-dimensional Kitaev chain which incorporates both time-reversal symmetry (TRS) breaking and long-range interaction, sandwiched between two metallic leads from two sides. In this hybrid device, we study electrical transport under voltage bias for varying strength of the TRS breaking phase. We compare the transport characteristics of long-range type Kitaev chain with that of the short-range Kitaev chain as the strength of the TRS breaking phase varies. We find that the TRS breaking modifies the density of states and localisation/delocalisation property of the eigenstates which in turn affect the transport characteristics. Moreover, we find that the impact of the TRS breaking is not identical for the long-range Kitaev chain and its short-range counterpart. Therefore, noticeable differences in the transport properties can be observed due to the interplay between the TRS breaking and the range of interaction.

AI.tldr: This paper studies electrical transport in a hybrid device with an extended one-dimensional Kitaev chain (including TRS breaking and long-range interaction) between two metallic leads, finding that TRS breaking alters density of states and localization, and its effects differ between long-range and short-range Kitaev chains.

AI.method: The authors construct a hybrid device with an extended 1D Kitaev chain (with TRS breaking and long-range interaction) sandwiched between two metallic leads, and analyze electrical transport under voltage bias while varying the TRS breaking phase strength.
AI.result: TRS breaking modifies the density of states and localization/delocalization of eigenstates, affecting transport. The impact differs between long-range and short-range Kitaev chains, leading to noticeable differences in transport properties due to the interplay between TRS breaking and interaction range.
AI.conclusion: The interplay between time-reversal symmetry breaking and the range of interaction (long-range vs. short-range) produces distinct transport characteristics in Kitaev chain junctions.

title: Phonon-driven Floquet-Bloch states probed by quantum beat spectroscopy
summary: Controlling material excitations offers access to novel fundamental and technological properties. The paradigm of Floquet engineering, the manipulation of the electronic structure using a coherent and time-periodic driving source, has attracted significant attention. While most realizations rely on strong optical fields, coherent phonons provide an alternative route to realizing Floquet-Bloch states, and are expected to enable substantially longer-lived Floquet-Bloch states. We show that laser-excited coherent phonons drive Floquet-Bloch states. Using time-resolved multiphoton photoemission combined with quantum beat spectroscopy on graphene-covered Ir(111), we track the coherent electronic dynamics of the image-potential states dressed by coherent phonons. The beat signal indicates the presence of sideband structure with the coherent-phonon frequency as its fundamental period, consistent with Floquet theory. Furthermore, an independent oscillation in intensity at the same frequency was observed, confirming excitation of the coherent phonon mode. Compared with conventional light-driven Floquet-Bloch states, the observed phonon-driven Floquet-Bloch states persist for one to two orders of magnitude longer. These results establish a time-domain route to identifying phonon-driven Floquet-Bloch states and reveal their formation on ultrafast timescales.

An independent intensity oscillation at the same frequency confirmed coherent phonon excitation. The phonon-driven Floquet-Bloch states persisted 1-2 orders of magnitude longer than light-driven counterparts.
AI.conclusion: The results establish a time-domain route to identifying phonon-driven Floquet-Bloch states and reveal their ultrafast formation dynamics, offering a pathway toward substantially longer-lived Floquet-engineered electronic states.

title: Topological control of third-harmonic generation in a mesoscopic quantum ring with spiral dislocation
comment: 14 pages, 12 figures, 1 table. Comments are welcome
summary: We investigate the nonlinear optical response of a two-dimensional mesoscopic quantum ring subjected to a spiral dislocation, with emphasis on third-harmonic generation (THG). The topological defect is modeled through a torsion-induced deformation of space, which modifies the effective metric without introducing curvature. By combining the minimal-coupling prescription in curved space with a radial ring confinement and a perpendicular magnetic field, we derive the effective radial Schrödinger problem, obtain the bound states, and evaluate the nonlinear susceptibilities within the electric-dipole approximation. We show that the axial symmetry of the topologically deformed ring preserves the dipole selection rule $Δm=\pm 1$ and therefore suppresses second-harmonic generation, while THG remains allowed through multistep transition chains. The study is further expanded through three complementary analyses that can be implemented without changing the Hamiltonian: a dephasing-controlled study of spectral resolution, three-dimensional waterfall spectra showing the dependence on $β$ and $B$, and a channel-resolved decomposition of the THG amplitude. Together, these results establish the spiral dislocation as a robust geometric knob for tuning nonlinear optical activity in mesoscopic ring-shaped nanostructures.

title: A parsimonious structure model for the icosahedral quasicrystal Cd5.7Yb
comment: Accepted by Acta Cryst. A, June 22, 2026
summary: A compact structure model for the icosahedral phase Cd5.7Yb is presented. The model is based on a higher-dimensional description and a cut-and-projection procedure to generate the atom distribution in three-dimensional physical space. It strictly employs only spherical or elliptical occupation domains, ensuring a low number of parameters and low calculation cost. In the presented form the model has seven adjustable parameters. Despite its minimalistic setting, the model reproduces available experimental data, such as chemical composition, mass density and electron density distribution, as well as the cluster structure in physical space very well. Nevertheless, the approximation of the occupation domains by spheres and ellipses evidently implies limitations in accuracy and universality. The model can be adapted for the description of other Tsai-type icosahedral phases.

AI.tldr: A compact 7-parameter model for the icosahedral phase Cd5.7Yb using spherical/elliptical occupation domains and cut-and-projection method, reproducing experimental data well despite accuracy limitations.
AI.motivation: To develop a low-parameter, computationally efficient structural model for the icosahedral phase Cd5.7Yb based on higher-dimensional description and cut-and-projection procedure.

AI.result: The model successfully reproduces experimental data including chemical composition, mass density, electron density distribution, and cluster structure in physical space, despite limitations in accuracy and universality from spherical/elliptical approximations.
AI.conclusion: The model offers a compact minimalistic description of Cd5.7Yb icosahedral phase and can be adapted for other Tsai-type icosahedral phases, though spherical/elliptical occupation domains impose accuracy constraints.

title: Heat rectification through a quantum two-level system
summary: We study heat rectification through a quantum two-level system asymmetrically coupled to two thermal baths, as described by the Ohmic spin-boson model. We evaluate the steady-state heat current using a tensor-network approach, which enables us to access the strongly correlated regime, and benchmark the results against analytical formulas in several limiting regimes, including the weak-coupling and incoherent-tunneling regimes. We identify a scaling regime where the studied system flows from an ultraviolet regime, at temperatures larger than the Kondo temperature, to an infrared regime, at temperatures lower than the Kondo temperature. By applying perturbation theory near the infrared fixed point, we find that the rectification ratio follows a universal power law. Our numerical results agree well with this analytical prediction. Our results provide a fundamental understanding of how dissipation-induced many-body physics affects heat transport.

Using tensor-network methods to access strongly correlated regimes and benchmarking against analytical formulas, the authors identify a scaling regime flowing from ultraviolet to infrared temperatures relative to the Kondo temperature. They derive a universal power law for the rectification ratio near the infrared fixed point, which is validated by numerical results, providing fundamental insights into how dissipation-induced many-body physics impacts heat transport.
